topics.description: Know the range of genres in which students are assessed (essays, critiques, explanations, exercises, case studies, literature surveys, methodology recounts such as lab reports, research reports, proposals, design specifications, problem questions, and narrative or reflective recounts) and the broad social purposes they serve, from demonstrating knowledge to preparing for professional practice. This map helps learners recognise what an assignment is asking for and see that the essay is not the only, or even the dominant, genre in many disciplines.
masteryEvidence: Classifies a set of real assignment briefs by genre family and states the social purpose each serves
Explains why the same command word (for example 'discuss') can appear in briefs for different genres
Identifies which genre families predominate in their own discipline and level of study
Recognises when an assignment label names one genre but the brief and criteria require features of another, and seeks clarification
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner six anonymised assignment briefs from different disciplines. Ask them to sort the briefs into genre families and say, for each, what the marker most wants to see. Check whether sorting is based on purpose and expected structure rather than on subject or title alone.

topics.name: Argumentative essay
topics.description: Produce a thesis-led essay that takes a defensible position on a contested question and builds a cumulative, source-supported case for it, engaging with alternative views and qualifying the position where the evidence requires. Typical stages are an introduction that frames the issue and states the thesis, body paragraphs that each advance a reason with evidence and commentary, treatment of counter-positions, and a conclusion that answers the question in the light of the argument; characteristic language includes stance markers, hedges and boosters, concession–counter patterns and evaluative reporting of sources.
masteryEvidence: States a specific, arguable thesis that directly answers the question and develops it, rather than merely repeating it, across the essay
Orders body paragraphs so that each sub-claim contributes to the overall case, with explicit links back to the thesis
Supports claims with relevant, attributed source evidence and explains how the evidence supports each claim
Represents at least one serious counter-position fairly and concedes or rebuts it with reasons
Calibrates claim strength to the evidence with hedges and boosters
Writes a conclusion that answers the question and states the limits or implications of the position
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an essay question and 20 minutes to produce a thesis statement, three topic sentences and one counter-argument with a response. Check that the thesis takes a position, that the topic sentences advance distinct reasons for it rather than naming topics, and that the counter-argument is a credible objection answered with a reason rather than dismissed.

topics.name: Discussion essay
topics.description: Produce an essay that represents two or more perspectives on an issue fairly, weighs them against evidence and explicit criteria, and reaches a reasoned, qualified conclusion. Typical stages are statement of the issue, presentation of perspectives (in blocks or point by point), evaluation and judgement; characteristic language includes attribution and reporting verbs, contrastive connectors, concession and evaluative lexis. In UK higher education even a 'discuss' essay is usually expected to arrive at a position, and often to signal it early.
masteryEvidence: Represents each perspective accurately and with comparable care, attributing views to their sources
Organises perspectives point by point or in blocks and can justify the choice
Evaluates perspectives against explicit criteria or evidence rather than simply juxtaposing them
Keeps their own evaluation linguistically distinguishable from reported views
Reaches a conclusion that follows from the weighing and is appropriately qualified
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 'Discuss' question and two short sources holding opposing views. Ask for an outline plan and the concluding paragraph. Check that the plan includes an evaluative stage, that both views are represented fairly, and that the conclusion takes a qualified position derived from the weighing rather than stating that both sides have advantages.

topics.name: Compare-and-contrast essay
topics.description: Produce an essay that compares two or more theories, cases, methods, policies or texts against explicit criteria and uses the comparison to make a point, such as which option is more appropriate or what a difference reveals, rather than listing similarities and differences. Typical stages are introduction of the items and the basis of comparison, criterion-led (point-by-point) or item-led (block) comparison, evaluation of the significance of the differences, and a conclusion stating the outcome; characteristic language includes comparative structures, contrastive connectors and hedged evaluative claims.
masteryEvidence: Selects comparison criteria relevant to the question and states them explicitly in the introduction
Organises the body point by point or in blocks and keeps the chosen pattern consistent and cross-referenced
Uses accurate comparative structures and contrastive connectors to express degrees of similarity and difference
Explains the significance of differences for the question rather than only recording them
Concludes with a judgement or insight that the comparison supports
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a table comparing two items on four features and ask for a 150-word paragraph plus a one-sentence thesis. Check that the paragraph is organised by criterion, uses precise comparative language (for example 'considerably higher than', 'whereas'), and that the thesis states what the comparison shows.

topics.name: Explanation and cause–effect essay
topics.description: Produce an essay that explains how or why a phenomenon occurs: its causes (factorial explanation), its consequences (consequential explanation) or the mechanism or sequence by which it happens, evaluating the relative importance and certainty of the factors. Typical stages are identification of the phenomenon, an explanation sequence organised by factor, consequence or step, and a conclusion that weighs the factors; characteristic language includes causal verbs and nouns (lead to, result in, a consequence of), nominalised causal chains, hedged causal claims and sequencing.
masteryEvidence: Identifies whether a question calls for causes, consequences or a mechanism and organises the essay accordingly
Groups causal factors into categories and sequences them by importance or chronology with explicit justification
Explains the mechanism by which a factor produces an effect rather than only naming the factor
Uses causal verbs, nouns and prepositions accurately, including nominalised causal chains
Hedges causal claims that rest on correlational evidence and concludes by weighing factors rather than restating them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write the introduction and one body paragraph for 'Explain the main causes of X' using a short source pack. Check whether the introduction maps the factors, whether the paragraph explains a mechanism rather than just naming a cause, and whether causal claims are hedged to suit the evidence.

topics.name: Problem–solution essay
topics.description: Produce an essay that defines a problem, establishes its causes and significance, presents possible responses and evaluates them against criteria such as effectiveness, feasibility, cost and equity, ending with a justified recommendation. The genre realises the situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern; characteristic language includes problem-signalling nouns (challenge, barrier, shortfall), evaluative lexis, conditional and hypothetical reasoning, and recommending language.
masteryEvidence: Defines the problem precisely, establishing its scope and significance with evidence
Presents more than one response and evaluates each against stated criteria
Uses conditional and hypothetical language to discuss the likely effects of proposed responses
Recommends a response and justifies it in relation to the criteria and the limitations of alternatives
Uses problem and evaluation signalling nouns that make the pattern visible to the reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short case describing a campus or community problem and ask for one paragraph evaluating a proposed solution. Check that the paragraph applies at least two explicit criteria, acknowledges a limitation or trade-off and uses conditional language for predicted effects.

topics.name: Examination essay
topics.description: Write an essay under timed, usually closed-book conditions that answers the set question directly from revised knowledge, with a clear position, a quickly planned structure and selective use of remembered evidence. Compared with coursework essays, examiners typically expect a compact introduction, sustained relevance and less precisely referenced sources; expectations about citation, length and structure vary by department and should be checked in past papers, examiners' comments and module guidance.
masteryEvidence: Decodes the question's command words, scope and implied structure within the first minutes and plans accordingly
Allocates time across questions in proportion to marks and leaves time to check
States a direct answer to the question in the introduction and returns to it in each paragraph
Selects revised content that serves the argument rather than reproducing everything remembered
Refers to scholars, theories and evidence with the degree of precision expected locally in exams (for example author and approximate date)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set an unseen question from a past paper in the learner's subject area with 40 minutes' writing time. Check the first paragraph for a direct answer, whether body paragraphs stay relevant to the question rather than reproducing pre-learned material, and whether the essay is complete and visibly planned.

topics.name: Short-answer responses
topics.description: Write concise, accurate answers, from a sentence to a paragraph, that define, identify, explain or briefly justify, as required in coursework exercises, short-answer exam questions and in-class tests. Markers reward precision, correct terminology and completeness relative to the marks available rather than introductions or elaboration; typical language includes formal definitions, compact causal and procedural explanation, and dense noun phrases.
masteryEvidence: Answers the question in the first sentence without restating it or adding an introduction
Scales the length and number of points to the marks available
Uses discipline terminology accurately and gives formal definitions where the question requires them
Includes the explanation step (how or why) when the command word requires more than identification
Adds an example or brief evidence only where it earns credit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three short-answer questions worth 2, 4 and 6 marks on content they have studied. Check whether answer length and number of points scale with the marks, whether the first sentence answers directly, and whether 'explain' items include a reason or mechanism rather than a bare identification.

topics.name: Critical review of an article
topics.description: Write a review of a single research article or theoretical text that summarises its aims, approach and main claims accurately and concisely, then evaluates it against appropriate criteria (such as quality of evidence, methodological soundness, coherence of argument, contribution and relevance) and reaches a balanced overall judgement. Typical stages are context and purpose, summary, evaluation of strengths and limitations, and conclusion; characteristic language includes evaluative reporting verbs, mitigated criticism, praise–criticism pairs and hedged judgements.
masteryEvidence: Summarises the text's purpose, approach and main claims accurately, in the proportion the brief requires
Evaluates against explicit criteria suited to the text type rather than personal agreement or disagreement
Supports each evaluative point with specific reference to the text and, where useful, to other literature
Balances strengths and limitations and mitigates criticism appropriately
Reaches an overall judgement about the text's value for a stated purpose or reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract and methods section of a short empirical article and ask for one evaluative paragraph. Check that the evaluation targets a specific feature (for example the sample or a measure), explains its consequence for the authors' claims, and is phrased with appropriate mitigation rather than as dismissal or unexplained praise.

topics.name: Book review
topics.description: Write a review of a scholarly book for an academic readership that situates the book in its field, describes its aims, scope and structure selectively, evaluates its argument, evidence and contribution, and recommends it, or not, to specified readers. Unlike an article critique set as coursework, a published book review is a public evaluative act within a discipline: reviewers balance and often mitigate criticism, and follow venue conventions on length, structure and bibliographic header.
masteryEvidence: Situates the book in relation to its field and the debates it addresses
Describes the book's aims and structure selectively, foregrounding what the evaluation needs
Evaluates contribution, argument and evidence with specific reference to chapters or claims
Balances praise and criticism and mitigates criticism to suit the venue
Identifies the intended readership and recommends the book to them with reasons
Follows the conventions of a target journal or brief for length, headings and bibliographic details
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give learners two published book reviews from a journal in their field. Ask them to mark where the reviewer evaluates, how criticism is softened and to whom the book is recommended, then to write the closing recommendation paragraph for a book they know. Check for a balanced, reasoned judgement addressed to a specified readership.

topics.name: Reflective writing
topics.description: Write structured reflection that describes a significant experience selectively, examines one's responses and assumptions, analyses the experience using relevant theory or evidence, and draws conclusions for future practice or learning. Assessed in education, health, business, engineering and EAP itself, the genre combines first-person, past-tense recount with present-tense analysis and future-oriented action planning; markers usually reward depth of analysis and links to theory rather than description or disclosure, and briefs differ widely on structure and citation.
masteryEvidence: Selects a specific, significant incident and describes it concisely as a basis for analysis
Moves from description to analysis by explaining why events unfolded as they did and questioning their own assumptions
Links the experience to relevant theory, research or professional standards
Uses first person, tense shifts and hedged interpretation appropriately across reflective stages
Formulates specific, realistic actions for future practice that follow from the analysis
Uses a reflective model as a scaffold without letting it dictate a formulaic text, following the local brief on structure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two short reflective paragraphs on the same incident, one largely descriptive and one analytical. Ask which would gain higher marks and why, then ask them to add two sentences to the weaker one. Check whether the additions interpret the experience, link it to theory or evidence, or derive a future action, rather than adding narrative or emotion.

topics.name: Annotated bibliography
topics.description: Compile an annotated bibliography in which each correctly formatted reference is followed by a concise annotation that summarises the source's purpose, approach and main findings or argument and, depending on the brief, evaluates its quality and explains its relevance to the writer's project. The genre isolates and trains selective summarising, source evaluation and relevance judgement; annotations are usually short paragraphs, report the source's claims with present-tense reporting verbs and mark evaluative and relevance comments as the writer's own.
masteryEvidence: Formats each entry accurately in the required referencing style
Summarises each source's purpose, approach and key claims concisely without reproducing its abstract
Evaluates each source with explicit criteria suited to its type (for example authority, evidence, currency)
Explains how each source will be used in the writer's project where the brief requires it
Keeps descriptive, evaluative and relevance comments distinguishable within each annotation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a journal article (or its abstract and methods) and a stated project focus, and ask for an annotation of about 150 words. Check that the annotation does not reproduce the abstract, includes a reasoned evaluation, states relevance to the project and is preceded by an accurate reference.

topics.name: Literature review assignment
topics.description: Write a coursework literature review, stand-alone or as a section of a larger assignment, that maps and synthesises the literature on a defined question thematically, evaluates the strength and limits of the evidence, identifies agreements, tensions and gaps, and positions a question or argument in relation to them. Typical stages are scope and rationale, thematic sections in which sources are placed in dialogue, and a conclusion summarising the state of knowledge and its gaps; characteristic language includes varied integral and non-integral citation, evaluative reporting verbs, comparison, and the present perfect for the state of a field.
masteryEvidence: Defines and justifies the scope of the review and, where required, the search approach
Organises the review by themes, debates or methods rather than source by source
Synthesises several sources within paragraphs, showing agreement, disagreement and qualification
Evaluates the evidence base rather than only reporting it
Identifies gaps or tensions that follow from the review and states their significance for the question
Maintains authorial voice through topic sentences and commentary that frame the cited material
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give learners five short source summaries on one question and 25 minutes to write one synthesis paragraph and one sentence identifying a gap. Check whether the paragraph is led by the writer's point, relates at least three sources to each other and evaluates them, and whether the gap follows from the synthesis rather than being asserted.

topics.name: Summary–response paper
topics.description: Write a paper that first summarises a source text accurately and even-handedly, then responds to it with a reasoned position (agreeing, disagreeing, qualifying or applying it to another context) supported by reasons and evidence. The genre makes explicit the boundary between reporting another writer's ideas and evaluating them and is a common bridge from reading to source-based argument; characteristic language includes attributive signal phrases and reporting verbs in the summary, and stance markers and concession in the response.
masteryEvidence: Summarises the source's main argument accurately in their own words, attributing it throughout
Separates summary from response clearly, without slipping evaluation into the summary
States a clear response position and supports it with reasons, examples or other sources
Engages with specific claims in the source rather than with its topic in general
Chooses reporting verbs that represent the source's stance accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 400-word opinion article and 40 minutes for a 300-word summary–response. Check that the summary is accurate, attributed and even-handed, that the response engages a specific claim from the source, and that the boundary between the two parts is clearly signalled.

topics.name: Report conventions
topics.description: Understand how academic and professional reports typically differ from essays: they respond to a defined problem, question or brief for a specified reader, are divided into numbered, headed sections that support selective reading, separate findings from interpretation, integrate captioned tables and figures, and often end with conclusions and recommendations. Section names and order vary widely across lab, project, business, technical and policy reports, so learners need to read the brief and departmental templates rather than assume a single report format.
masteryEvidence: Explains the main differences in purpose, reader and organisation between an essay and a report on the same topic
Uses informative headings and a consistent numbering system that supports selective reading
Separates presentation of findings from discussion or interpretation where the report type requires it
Integrates numbered, captioned tables and figures and refers to each in the text
Identifies the required sections and their order from a brief or template and adapts when they differ from a taught model
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an essay-style answer to a task whose brief specifies a report. Ask them to outline how it should be restructured, with section headings. Check whether the headings are informative and functional, whether findings are separated from interpretation and recommendations, and whether the learner cites the brief to justify the structure.

topics.name: Laboratory report
topics.description: Write a laboratory report that records and interprets a practical investigation, typically with an introduction stating the relevant theory and the aim or hypothesis, a method, results presented in tables and figures with data commentary, a discussion that interprets the results against theory and expected values and evaluates sources of error and uncertainty, and a conclusion. Although it resembles the IMRaD research article, the student lab report usually serves to demonstrate understanding of established theory, procedure and data handling, often for an experiment with a known outcome, and its sections, tense and voice conventions vary with discipline, module and lab manual.
masteryEvidence: States the aim and the theory needed to interpret the experiment concisely, linking them to the expected outcome
Describes the method in enough detail for replication, using tense and voice according to the local convention
Presents results in correctly numbered and labelled tables and figures, with commentary that highlights significant patterns and values
Interprets results against theory or expected values, quantifying discrepancies and evaluating specific sources of error and uncertainty
Follows the structure and formatting specified in the lab manual or brief
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the aim, a small dataset and one figure from a simple experiment. Ask for a results paragraph and a discussion paragraph. Check that the results paragraph highlights significant patterns with values and refers to the figure without interpreting, and that the discussion compares outcomes with theory and evaluates specific sources of error rather than generic 'human error'.

topics.name: Empirical project report
topics.description: Write a report of a small-scale empirical study that the student has designed and conducted (for example a survey, interview study, observation or small experiment), presenting the rationale and research questions, a focused review of literature, methods with justification and ethical considerations, findings, a discussion relating findings to the literature, limitations and conclusions. Common on pre-sessional extended projects and in undergraduate and master's research modules, the genre apprentices learners into research reporting; its sections, length and quantitative or qualitative conventions vary by discipline and brief.
masteryEvidence: Formulates focused, answerable research questions and keeps methods, findings and conclusions aligned with them
Justifies methodological choices such as sampling, instruments and analysis, and reports ethical procedures
Presents findings accurately using quantitative or qualitative reporting conventions appropriate to the design
Discusses findings in relation to the reviewed literature, explaining agreements and differences
States limitations proportionately and draws conclusions that do not overreach the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the research questions, a method summary, a findings table and an overclaiming conclusion from a student project. Ask them to identify misalignments and rewrite the conclusion. Check whether they spot claims that the sample and design cannot support and revise them with appropriate hedging and scope.

topics.name: Case study analysis
topics.description: Write a case study analysis that applies disciplinary concepts, theories or frameworks to a real or hypothetical case (an organisation, patient, client, project, school or event) to diagnose the key issues, evaluate options and, usually, recommend action. Typical stages are a brief case overview, identification and prioritisation of issues, analysis through theory or frameworks, evaluation of options, and recommendations, sometimes with implementation; the text may be report-like with headings or essay-like, and conventions differ sharply across business, health, law, education and engineering.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the key issues in a case and prioritises them with justification
Applies relevant concepts or frameworks analytically, using case evidence, rather than describing the framework
Distinguishes case facts from inferences and assumptions
Evaluates options against criteria and recommends action that follows from the analysis
Uses the format, headings and depth of theory specified by the brief
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page case and a named framework or theory from their discipline. Ask for one analytical paragraph applying it to one issue. Check whether case facts are used as evidence, whether the framework is applied rather than defined at length, and whether the paragraph moves towards a judgement or implication.

topics.name: Business report
topics.description: Write a business report that investigates an organisational problem or opportunity for a specified decision-maker, analyses relevant evidence and data (often with management frameworks), presents findings and conclusions, and makes prioritised, feasible recommendations. Typical sections include an executive summary, introduction with terms of reference, findings or analysis, conclusions, recommendations and appendices; because the reader is assumed to be busy and decision-oriented, front-loading, informative headings and visuals matter, and assignment briefs often simulate a client or manager.
masteryEvidence: Defines the purpose, terms of reference and readership of the report
Analyses evidence and data relevant to the problem, using frameworks analytically rather than as lists
Distinguishes findings, conclusions and recommendations and keeps them aligned
Writes specific, prioritised and feasible recommendations with justification and, where required, implementation steps
Uses headings, numbering, visuals and an executive summary that a decision-maker could act on
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the findings and conclusions sections of a short business report and ask for three recommendations. Check whether each recommendation follows from a conclusion, is specific about who should do what and when, is prioritised, and acknowledges cost or risk.

topics.name: Technical and design report
topics.description: Write a technical or design report that documents an engineering, computing or design project: the problem and requirements or specification, constraints, generation and evaluation of options against criteria, the selected design and its justification, implementation, testing or validation against requirements, and evaluation with recommendations for further work. The reader must be able to follow, assess and potentially reproduce decisions, so the genre relies on precise technical description, requirement and specification language, comparative evaluation, and close integration of diagrams, tables and calculations.
masteryEvidence: States requirements and constraints in precise, testable terms
Describes design options and evaluates them against explicit criteria, justifying the selected solution and its trade-offs
Describes components, structures and processes accurately with integrated, labelled diagrams
Reports testing or validation results and evaluates performance against the requirements
Follows departmental and professional conventions for numbered sections, appendices and technical notation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a design requirement and data on two candidate solutions. Ask for a design-selection paragraph. Check for explicit criteria linked to the requirements, quantitative comparison, justification of trade-offs and reference to a numbered table or figure.

topics.name: Project proposal (student)
topics.description: Write a proposal for a student project or dissertation that defines the topic and research questions or aims, justifies them in relation to the literature and a gap or practical need, outlines methods and data sources, addresses ethics and feasibility, and presents a realistic timeline. The proposal persuades a supervisor or module team that the project is worthwhile, answerable and achievable; characteristic language includes future and conditional forms, purpose and justification expressions, and hedged statements about expected outcomes.
masteryEvidence: States focused research questions or aims and justifies their significance with reference to literature or need
Identifies the gap, problem or need that the project addresses
Outlines methods and data sources that can answer the questions, with an analysis approach
Addresses ethical issues and feasibility, including access, time and resources
Presents a realistic timeline aligned with institutional deadlines
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a weak proposal with broad aims and a method that cannot answer them. Ask them to list the three most important revisions. Check whether they target alignment between aims and methods, feasibility within the time available, and justification of significance.

topics.name: Executive summary
topics.description: Write an executive summary that lets a decision-maker grasp a report's purpose, key findings, conclusions and recommendations without reading the full document. It stands alone, usually appears at the front, is short relative to the report, orders content by importance to the reader rather than by the report's section order, and states recommendations explicitly; unlike an academic abstract, it foregrounds implications and actions over method.
masteryEvidence: Includes purpose, key findings, conclusions and recommendations in proportion to their importance for the reader
Produces a text that can be understood without the full report, defining any essential terms
Front-loads the main message and orders content by importance to the decision-maker
Keeps within the specified length and introduces no information absent from the report
Explains how an executive summary differs from an abstract and from an introduction
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 1,500-word report and ask for a 200-word executive summary. Check that the main message appears in the first two sentences, that recommendations are explicit, that no new information is introduced and that method detail is minimal.

topics.name: Policy brief
topics.description: Write a short, evidence-based document that presents a policy problem, summarises and weighs the relevant evidence, sets out options with their trade-offs and recommends action to a non-specialist policy audience such as officials, practitioners or NGOs. Typical features are a front-loaded set of key messages, a concise problem statement, accessible synthesis of research with its strength signalled, options, and concrete recommendations addressed to named actors, presented in a few pages with headings and visuals; tone is authoritative but calibrated to the evidence, and organisations use their own templates.
masteryEvidence: States the policy problem and its significance concisely for a non-specialist reader
Synthesises research evidence accessibly while signalling its strength and limits
Presents options with trade-offs and recommends specific, feasible actions for named actors
Front-loads key messages and uses headings, visuals and plain language appropriately
Keeps recommendations within what the evidence supports, presenting risks and effect sizes in terms readers can interpret
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract and main findings of a policy-relevant research article and ask for a three-point 'key messages' box for a government official. Check that the messages are accessible, specific and action-oriented, that they do not overstate the evidence, and that any statistics are expressed in interpretable terms (for example absolute rather than only relative change).

topics.name: Professional practice portfolio
topics.description: Compile and write a professional practice portfolio for a placement, practicum or work-based module: dated logs of activities, reflective accounts of significant incidents, and evidence mapped to professional standards or competencies, held together by a commentary that synthesises development and plans further learning. Assessed in nursing and allied health, teacher education, social work, engineering and business placements, the genre combines factual recording, reflection and evidence-based argument, requires strict attention to confidentiality, and follows highly specific institutional and professional-body templates.
masteryEvidence: Maintains concise, factual, dated logs using appropriate professional terminology
Writes reflective accounts that link practice incidents to theory and to the relevant professional standards
Selects and annotates evidence that demonstrates specific competencies, explaining how each item meets them
Anonymises people and settings and observes confidentiality requirements
Synthesises development over the placement and sets specific goals for further learning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner one competency statement from a relevant professional standard and three items of evidence of varying relevance. Ask them to select the best item and write a 100-word annotation explaining how it demonstrates the competency. Check for explicit mapping, specificity and acknowledgement of what the evidence does not show.

topics.name: Academic blogs and public-facing writing
topics.description: Write academic blog posts, opinion pieces and other outreach texts that communicate research or disciplinary perspectives to non-specialist or mixed readers. Compared with academic genres, these texts lead with the main point, use a more personal and engaging voice, concrete examples, short paragraphs and links rather than formal citation, and signal uncertainty without technical hedging; they also require judgements about representing evidence fairly, the writer's public identity and platform norms.
masteryEvidence: Leads with a significant or newsworthy point and sustains it for a non-specialist reader
Explains technical concepts accessibly without distorting the evidence or overstating certainty
Uses an engaging voice, reader address and concrete examples suited to the platform
Attributes sources through links or brief references according to platform conventions
Adapts an academic text, such as their own assignment or an article, into a public-facing piece
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract of a published study and ask for a 150-word blog opening. Check for an opening that states why the finding matters, accessible explanation of the finding, appropriate signalling of uncertainty and absence of unexplained jargon.

topics.name: Undergraduate and master's dissertation
topics.description: Understand and plan the undergraduate or taught master's dissertation as a genre: an extended, largely independent piece of research or scholarship whose typical macrostructures include empirical IMRaD-like chapters, topic-based or theoretical structures and practice-based variants, with expectations of scope, length and originality that are lower than for doctoral theses. Learners need to see how proposal, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion and conclusion form one argument across chapters, and how supervision and assessment work; because expectations vary across disciplines and institutions, the handbook, marking criteria and past dissertations are the key sources.
masteryEvidence: Describes the macrostructure expected in their department and justifies any variation for their own project
Distinguishes taught-programme dissertation expectations of scope, originality and length from those of doctoral theses
Plans chapter functions and word allocations aligned with the research questions
Uses chapter introductions, conclusions and cross-references to guide the reader through the extended text
Uses handbook criteria and past dissertations to identify what distinguishes high-graded work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to produce a one-page chapter plan with word allocations and a one-sentence function for each chapter, based on their department's handbook. Check alignment with the research questions, realistic proportions (for example a discussion that is not squeezed), and whether functions state what each chapter does rather than what it is about.

topics.name: Abstracts for student work
topics.description: Write an abstract for a dissertation, project report or poster that summarises, in a stand-alone paragraph within a strict word limit, the context or problem, aim, method, main findings and conclusion or implication. Student abstracts follow moves similar to those of research abstracts but are judged mainly on accuracy, completeness and concision; tense typically shifts between present for context and conclusions and past for methods and findings, and some fields require structured formats with headings.
masteryEvidence: Includes the moves required by the brief (context, aim, method, findings, conclusion) in sensible proportion
Reports specific findings rather than promising that results 'will be discussed'
Uses tense and voice consistently with move function and local convention
Writes within the word limit without unexplained abbreviations, or citations unless permitted
Ensures the abstract matches the content and the strength of claims in the full text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 250-word abstract that ends indicatively ('results are discussed') and omits the method. Ask them to identify the missing moves and rewrite it in 200 words. Check for an added method, specific findings and a conclusion consistent with those findings.

topics.name: IMRaD and its variants
topics.description: Recognise the Introduction–Methods–Results–Discussion macrostructure as a conventional way of reporting empirical research, explain what each section does for the reader, and identify the variants used in one's own field, such as merged Results and Discussion, a separate Conclusions section, a theory section before Methods, or argument-led organisation in the humanities. Knowing the macrostructure lets writers put content where readers expect it, while recognising IMRaD as a disciplinary convention rather than a universal norm.
masteryEvidence: States the communicative purpose of each section of a research article from their own field in one sentence each
Identifies at least two departures from canonical IMRaD in a set of field-specific articles and names the function each variant serves
Relocates misplaced content in a draft, for example interpretation in Methods or new findings in Discussion, and justifies the move by section function
Explains why a theoretical, historical or practice-based paper may not use IMRaD, with reference to how that field makes knowledge claims
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three short articles from different fields (for example biochemistry, applied linguistics and history) with headings removed. Ask them to mark where each section begins and what it does. Check whether they reason from function (reporting procedure, presenting findings, interpreting) rather than from surface cues, and whether they treat the non-IMRaD article as differently organised rather than defective.

topics.name: Research article introductions
topics.description: Write research introductions that create a research space: establishing a territory (claiming centrality, generalising, reviewing previous research), establishing a niche, and occupying it by announcing the present research, its questions, and optionally its findings, value and structure. Writers adapt the model to their field and genre, including the cyclical moves, extended background and thesis-structure statements common in some disciplines and in PhD introductions, and they use it as an analytical lens on exemplars rather than as a fill-in template.
masteryEvidence: Annotates a published introduction from their own field for moves and steps, including recursive Move 1–Move 2 cycles where present
Writes an introduction in which the territory narrows towards the niche, the niche follows from cited work, and the announcement of the study answers the niche
Decides, with reference to field exemplars, whether to announce principal findings and outline the structure of the text in the introduction
Adapts the move structure for a thesis introduction, including statements of thesis structure, scope and definitions where expected
Explains how their discipline's introductions differ from the canonical CARS model and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a published introduction with its sentences jumbled. Ask them to reconstruct the order and label each sentence by move. Then ask which optional steps the author used and why. Check whether they rely on functional cues (generalisation, contrast, announcement) and whether they can justify optional steps by field convention.

topics.name: Literature review in research writing
topics.description: Write the literature review of a thesis, dissertation or article as an argument that positions the writer's own study: selecting and organising literature by theme, debate or problem, evaluating rather than merely reporting it, and building cumulatively towards the niche the study fills. Unlike a stand-alone coursework review, the research literature review is judged by how well it justifies the present study's questions, framework and design.
masteryEvidence: Organises the review around themes, debates or problems that map onto the study's questions, not around individual sources or chronology by default
Uses citation for a range of functions, including support, comparison, evaluation and application to the writer's own study, not attribution alone
Signals the writer's evaluative stance on bodies of work and individual studies while representing them fairly
Ends sections and the whole review with explicit links to the gap, framework or design of the present study
Justifies inclusion and exclusion of literature and, where relevant, describes how it was located
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring a draft review section and to state, in one sentence per paragraph, how that paragraph contributes to justifying their study. Check whether every paragraph can be linked to the questions, framework or design, whether the paragraphs contain evaluative commentary, and whether any paragraphs are source-by-source summaries with no positioning.

topics.name: Methods sections
topics.description: Write methods sections that describe the study (setting, participants or materials, instruments, procedures, data analysis) in enough detail for evaluation or replication and that establish credibility by justifying choices, citing precedents and addressing validity, reliability or trustworthiness. Move structure, level of detail, voice and the balance of description and justification vary considerably across disciplines and between laboratory, survey and qualitative traditions, so writers calibrate against field exemplars and reporting guidelines.
masteryEvidence: Includes the elements a reader in their field needs to evaluate or replicate the study, checked against an exemplar or reporting guideline
Justifies key design and analysis choices by rationale or precedent rather than only describing them
Orders information so that procedures are traceable, using sub-headings conventional in the field
Chooses voice, tense and agency appropriately, for example past passive or active 'we' for completed procedures and present tense for standard materials, according to field norms
Addresses validity, reliability or trustworthiness, and ethics approval where required, in the conventional place
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a methods paragraph that describes procedures without any justification. Ask them to identify the two decisions a reviewer would most likely question and to add one justification for each. Check whether they target consequential decisions such as sampling or analysis, and whether the justifications use rationale or cited precedent rather than restating the procedure.

topics.name: Results sections
topics.description: Present findings in a logical order that answers the research questions, using visuals and prose together: locating the reader in a table or figure, highlighting what is significant, and adding the degree of commentary the field allows (from minimal to substantial interpretation). Writers decide what to report in text and what to leave in visuals, separate reporting from interpretation where the genre requires it, and keep claims proportionate to the data.
masteryEvidence: Orders results by research question or by importance rather than in the order the analyses were run
Writes location statements and highlighting statements that select key patterns rather than repeating every value in a table
Adds commentary such as comparison, explanation or evaluation at the level typical of their field's results sections
Uses tense consistently, typically past for findings and present for what a table or figure shows
Keeps claims about results within what the data support, with appropriate hedging where findings are tentative
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a table with six to eight values and a research question. Ask for a 100-word results paragraph. Check whether they locate the table, select the two or three patterns relevant to the question, avoid restating every number, use tense appropriately and keep any comment proportionate to the data.

topics.name: Discussion sections
topics.description: Write discussion sections that move from results to meaning: restating key findings in relation to the research questions, comparing them with previous research, explaining expected and unexpected outcomes, evaluating the study's limitations, and drawing implications. Discussions are typically cyclical, repeating statement–comparison–explanation sequences for each major finding, and their persuasiveness depends on claims calibrated to the evidence and on alternative explanations considered rather than dismissed.
masteryEvidence: Organises the discussion around key findings or research questions, cycling through statement, comparison with literature and explanation for each
Relates each major finding explicitly to cited previous work, stating whether it confirms, extends, qualifies or contradicts it
Offers and weighs more than one possible explanation for unexpected findings
Calibrates the strength of interpretive claims to the design and data, using hedging and boosting deliberately
Draws implications for theory, practice or further research that follow from the findings rather than from the topic in general
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a results summary with one expected and one unexpected finding and two short abstracts of earlier studies. Ask for a discussion paragraph on the unexpected finding. Check whether they compare it with prior work, propose and evaluate at least two explanations, and hedge appropriately without either overclaiming or retreating into vagueness.

topics.name: Conclusions and implications
topics.description: Write concluding sections and chapters that consolidate the research: briefly restating aims and key findings, answering the research questions, articulating the contribution, drawing calibrated implications for theory, practice or policy, evaluating the study and recommending specific further research. In theses, the conclusion also looks across chapters and back to the field, and conventions vary on whether conclusions form a separate section in articles.
masteryEvidence: Answers each research question explicitly in the conclusion, using the same terms as the introduction
Synthesises findings into overall claims rather than repeating chapter summaries
Draws implications that follow from the findings and names who they matter to
Recommends further research with a specific focus and design rather than a generic call
Adjusts length and content to genre: an article conclusion, a dissertation chapter or a thesis conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read their conclusion alongside their research questions and mark where each question is answered. Then ask them to underline each implication and say which finding it comes from. Check for unanswered questions, implications with no basis in the findings and generic future-research statements.

topics.name: Research abstracts
topics.description: Write informative abstracts for articles, dissertations and theses that represent the whole study within a tight word limit, typically situating the research, stating its purpose, describing the method, summarising key results and stating conclusions or implications, either as continuous prose or under the headings of a structured abstract. Abstracts are read as stand-alone texts by searchers, editors and examiners, so they are both a summary and a promotional genre, and their move emphasis varies across disciplines and journals.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the moves present and absent in abstracts from their target journals or department
Writes an abstract within a set word limit that includes purpose, method, key results with specific findings, and a conclusion or implication
Writes a structured abstract to journal-specified headings when required
Uses tense and voice consistent with field abstracts, for example past tense for methods and results, present tense for conclusions
Removes citations, undefined abbreviations and background that does not serve the stand-alone reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a 150-word abstract of their own project in 20 minutes, then to label each sentence by move. Check whether results are stated specifically (not 'results are discussed'), whether a conclusion or implication is included, and whether background is proportionate.

topics.name: Writing about limitations
topics.description: Identify the limitations that genuinely affect how a study's findings can be interpreted (sample, design, measurement, analysis, scope) and write about them so that readers can judge the claims, by stating each limitation, its likely effect on the findings and, where possible, how it was mitigated or could be addressed. Well-written limitations protect the contribution by showing the writer's command of the design, whereas generic or apologetic lists undermine it.
masteryEvidence: Selects limitations that bear on the interpretation of this study's findings rather than listing generic ones such as 'small sample' without consequence
States the likely direction or scope of each limitation's effect on the findings
Pairs limitations with mitigation, counter-weighing strengths or specific future research where justified
Uses concessive and hedging language to acknowledge limitations without retracting the study's main claims
Places limitations where the field expects them, for example in the discussion, a dedicated sub-section or the conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a brief study description and a draft limitations paragraph that lists four generic weaknesses and apologises. Ask them to rewrite it. Check whether they keep only consequential limitations, explain how each affects interpretation, add mitigation or a future direction, and avoid both apology and dismissal.

topics.name: Research questions and hypotheses
topics.description: Formulate and present an aim, research questions and, where the design calls for them, hypotheses that are answerable, appropriately scoped and aligned with the stated gap and the chosen methods. Writers also choose how to present them, as numbered questions, objectives or a purpose statement, and use consistent wording across the introduction, methods and discussion. Well-formed questions are the reference point that examiners and reviewers use to judge the coherence of the whole study.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes an aim, an objective, a research question and a testable hypothesis, and selects the form suited to the design (exploratory, explanatory or confirmatory)
Rewrites a vague or yes/no question into one whose wording specifies population, phenomenon and the kind of answer sought
Checks that each question can be answered by the proposed data and analysis, and revises or drops questions that cannot
Keeps question wording stable across introduction, methods, results and discussion, or signals and justifies any change
Uses hypothesis language accurately, including directional predictions and null hypotheses where the field expects them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-paragraph study summary with three flawed research questions (one too broad, one yes/no with no analytic purchase, one not answerable from the data described). Ask them to diagnose and rewrite each. Check whether the rewrites are answerable with the described data, and whether the learner explains the misalignment rather than only changing the wording.

topics.name: Establishing a research gap
topics.description: Construct the textual case that a niche exists, through counter-claiming, indicating a gap, raising a question, continuing a tradition or adding to what is known, using the lexicogrammar that realises these moves: contrastive connectors, negative or restrictive quantifiers (few studies, little attention), present perfect for the state of research and evaluative lexis. The niche must follow from the literature reviewed and lead to the present study, and it should be stated with appropriate caution, since an overstated gap ('no research exists') is easily refuted.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the type of niche in published introductions (counter-claim, gap, question, continuation or extension) and the signalling language used
Writes a niche statement that is grounded in specific cited work rather than asserted in general terms
Calibrates gap claims, for example by limiting scope ('in this population', 'longitudinally') rather than claiming that nothing has been done
Links the niche explicitly to the aims or questions of the present study so that the study answers the gap it has opened
Varies niche-establishing resources (adversative connectors, negative quantifiers, contrastive evaluation) rather than relying on one formula
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short review paragraph (four or five cited studies) and ask them to write two to three sentences establishing a niche for a stated study. Check whether the gap is traceable to the cited studies, whether its scope is defensible, whether it leads directly to the stated aim, and whether the language is hedged and evaluative rather than absolute.

topics.name: Claiming contribution
topics.description: State what the research adds (new evidence, a new method, a new context, a theoretical refinement or a practical application) and why it matters, at a level of confidence the evidence supports. Writers relate the contribution explicitly to the niche established earlier, choose between self-mention and impersonal framing, and balance promotional and cautious language according to field and genre. Doctoral examiners and journal reviewers look for this statement, and its absence or overstatement is a common reason for criticism.
masteryEvidence: States the contribution in one or two sentences that a non-specialist in their department can understand
Classifies the contribution type (empirical, methodological, theoretical, contextual or practical) and words it accordingly
Links the contribution explicitly to the niche established in the introduction or literature review
Calibrates originality claims, avoiding unsupported 'first' and 'novel' claims while not hedging the contribution into invisibility
Uses self-mention or impersonal constructions deliberately, according to field and target genre
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to complete the frame 'This study contributes to … by …, which matters because …' for their own project, and then to point to where the matching niche appears in their introduction. Check whether the contribution is specific, of a named type, linked to the niche and calibrated.

topics.name: Thesis macrostructure
topics.description: Choose and justify an overall organisation for a dissertation or thesis — traditional simple (IMRaD-like), traditional complex (several studies), topic-based, or publication-based (compilation of articles with framing chapters) — and plan chapters that fit the research, the institution's regulations and disciplinary norms. Writers understand what each chapter type contributes, how a publication-based thesis builds coherence across stand-alone papers, and what examiners will look for in the whole document.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the macrostructure type of theses from their own department and relates it to the research design
Produces a chapter plan with each chapter's purpose, main claim and approximate length
Explains how their chosen structure presents a coherent argument across the whole document
For a publication-based thesis, plans the framing chapters and linking text that integrate the papers
Checks the plan against institutional regulations, for example word limits, required elements and rules for including co-authored work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to produce a one-page chapter plan and to explain why they chose this macrostructure rather than one alternative. Check whether the structure fits the design (single study, multiple studies, theory-led or by publication), whether each chapter has a stated purpose and whether regulatory constraints have been checked.

topics.name: Chapter introductions, conclusions and metatext
topics.description: Guide readers through a long document with metatext above the paragraph level: chapter introductions that state purpose and preview structure, chapter conclusions that summarise and link forward, cross-references between chapters, and sign-posting that reminds the reader how the current section serves the thesis argument. Writers calibrate the density of metatext so that it orients the reader without padding or repeating content.
masteryEvidence: Writes chapter introductions that state the chapter's purpose, its relation to the research questions and its structure
Writes chapter conclusions that summarise the chapter's claims and link explicitly to the next chapter
Uses accurate cross-references to other chapters and sections, including forward and backward references
Varies metatext language and keeps it proportionate, avoiding repetitive formulae and preview lists that duplicate headings
Revises metatext after restructuring so that previews and cross-references match the final document
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read only the chapter introductions and conclusions of their draft, in order, to a peer, who then summarises the thesis argument. Check whether the peer can reconstruct the argument, whether chapters link forward and back, and whether any previews or cross-references are inaccurate.

topics.name: Theoretical and conceptual frameworks
topics.description: Write a theoretical or conceptual framework section that explains which theories, models or concepts the study uses, why they were chosen over alternatives, how key constructs are defined and operationalised, and how the framework shapes the questions, data collection and analysis. The section should do analytical work later in the text rather than function as a free-standing summary of theory, and it should acknowledge disciplinary differences in whether and how frameworks are presented.
masteryEvidence: States which theory or set of concepts frames the study and justifies the choice against at least one plausible alternative
Defines key constructs and shows how each is operationalised or used analytically in the study
Distinguishes, in their own field's terms, between a theoretical framework, a conceptual framework and a literature review
Traces the framework's concepts forward into the analysis and discussion, for example as coding categories, variables or interpretive lenses
Represents theoretical sources accurately while making clear what the writer adopts, adapts or rejects
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to explain in two minutes how one named concept from their framework appears in their methods and in their findings. Check whether they can trace the concept into instruments, codes or variables and into interpretation; a learner who can only summarise the theory has written a description, not a framework.

topics.name: Reporting qualitative findings
topics.description: Present qualitative findings as an argued interpretation: organising them by theme or category, selecting and introducing participant extracts that illustrate and evidence analytic claims, commenting on each extract, and keeping the analyst's voice distinct from participants' voices. Writers show the range and prevalence of patterns without spurious counting, attend to negative cases, and present extracts ethically and consistently, with pseudonyms, transcription conventions and edits marked.
masteryEvidence: Frames each theme with an analytic claim before presenting supporting extracts, rather than letting quotations carry the argument
Introduces and follows extracts with commentary that explains what the extract shows and how it relates to the theme
Indicates how widespread a pattern is in principled ways and reports disconfirming or divergent cases
Separates participants' accounts from the writer's interpretation through attribution and reporting language
Applies consistent conventions for extract layout, identifiers, omissions and transcription
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three interview extracts and a theme label. Ask them to write one findings paragraph using two of the extracts. Check whether the paragraph opens with an analytic claim, whether each extract is framed and commented on, whether the analyst's voice is distinguishable from the participants', and whether the choice of extracts is justified.

topics.name: Reporting quantitative findings
topics.description: Report descriptive and inferential statistics in the conventional format of the field or style guide: test statistics, degrees of freedom, exact p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals in text and tables, with numbers, symbols and units styled correctly. Writers interpret statistical results in words a reader can follow, distinguish statistical significance from practical importance, and avoid the language of proof or of 'trends towards significance'.
masteryEvidence: Reports a statistical test in the format required by the target style (for example APA) with test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value and effect size
Accompanies each statistic with a plain-prose statement of what it shows in relation to the research question
Distinguishes statistical significance from the size or practical importance of an effect in the wording of claims
Avoids proof language and dichotomous misreadings of p-values, for example treating p = .06 as 'no effect' or as 'almost significant'
Designs tables with informative titles, notes and units, and does not duplicate table values in prose
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner raw output from a t-test or correlation and ask for one sentence reporting it and one interpreting it. Check the formatting (symbols, italics, decimals, exact p), the presence of an effect size, and whether the interpretation avoids 'proves' and does not equate non-significance with no difference.

topics.name: Research proposals
topics.description: Write proposals for doctoral admission, confirmation or funding that persuade reviewers a project is significant, original, feasible and well designed: establishing the problem and gap, stating aims and questions, outlining methods, timeline and resources, anticipating risks and ethics, and articulating expected contributions and benefits. Proposals are promissory and evaluative, written in future and conditional terms for readers who must decide quickly, and funders' templates and criteria shape their structure.
masteryEvidence: Writes a proposal whose aims, questions, methods and expected outcomes align in a way a reviewer can check quickly
Uses future and conditional forms and calibrated promissory language appropriate to work not yet done
Demonstrates feasibility through a realistic timeline, resources and risk-management statements
States expected contribution and wider benefit in terms that match the funder's or institution's criteria
Adapts structure and emphasis to a specific template, such as a doctoral application, a confirmation report or a funding call
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a funding call's assessment criteria and their own 500-word project summary. Ask them to mark where each criterion is addressed and to revise any section that does not address one. Check alignment between aims and methods, feasibility evidence and whether significance is stated for the specific audience.

topics.name: Ethics applications and participant documents
topics.description: Complete research ethics applications that describe procedures, risks, benefits, consent, confidentiality and data management accurately, and write participant information sheets and consent forms in plain, accessible and, where needed, translated language that enables genuinely informed consent. The genres serve two audiences, the ethics committee and participants, with different register demands, and they commit the researcher to procedures that later methods sections must match.
masteryEvidence: Describes procedures, risks and safeguards in an ethics application completely enough for a committee to assess them
Writes a participant information sheet in plain language, using short sentences, second-person address and no unexplained jargon
Includes the elements participants need, such as purpose, what taking part involves, voluntariness and withdrawal, data use and contacts, following the institution's template
Writes consent statements that are specific, separable where required and unambiguous
Keeps the methods, the ethics application and participant documents consistent with each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a jargon-heavy paragraph from a participant information sheet. Ask them to rewrite it for a lay participant. Check readability (sentence length, terminology, direct address), whether any information has been lost, and whether withdrawal and data-use statements are clear and accurate.

topics.name: Working with supervisors
topics.description: Manage the supervisory relationship through talk and writing: negotiating expectations, preparing agendas and submitting drafts with specific requests for feedback, interpreting and responding to written comments, disagreeing respectfully, and recording decisions and actions after meetings. Supervisory conventions vary across institutions, disciplines and individuals, so learners make these expectations explicit rather than assume them.
masteryEvidence: Discusses and records mutual expectations with the supervisor, for example meeting frequency, turnaround of drafts and type of feedback
Sends drafts with a cover note stating the stage of the draft and two or three specific questions
Prepares a meeting agenda and circulates a short record of decisions and actions afterwards
Interprets indirect feedback comments accurately and responds to each, stating what was changed or why not
Raises disagreement or concerns using mitigated, evidence-based language and knows the institutional routes for unresolved problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three authentic-style supervisor comments, one direct, one hedged ('you might want to consider…') and one cryptic ('?'), and ask what each requires and how they would respond. Check whether they recognise hedged comments as requests and whether they would clarify the cryptic one rather than ignore it.

topics.name: Sustaining thesis writing
topics.description: Sustain writing across a multi-year project by establishing regular, low-stakes writing routines, setting and monitoring realistic writing goals, using writing groups, retreats and accountability partners, separating generative writing from revision, and treating writing as part of doing research rather than as 'writing up' at the end. The aim is steady output and recovery from setbacks without compromising wellbeing.
masteryEvidence: Maintains a writing routine with planned sessions and records output over several weeks
Sets writing goals in terms of specific text, such as section drafts or word counts, rather than vague intentions
Uses at least one social structure for writing, such as a writing group, retreat or accountability partner
Writes from early in the project (notes, memos, draft sections) instead of postponing writing until the research is finished
Identifies personal patterns of avoidance or over-revision and adjusts strategies in response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show their writing log or calendar for the last month and to describe what happened in their least productive week. Check whether they have a routine, whether goals are text-specific, and whether they can identify a strategy to try next rather than attributing the problem to motivation alone.

topics.name: Writing positionality statements
topics.description: Write positionality and reflexivity statements that explain how the researcher's identities, experiences, relationships to participants and theoretical commitments may have shaped access, data and interpretation, and what was done about it. Effective statements are analytic and specific to the study rather than confessional or biographical, use first-person reference according to field conventions, and are integrated with methodological decisions rather than isolated in a separate box.
masteryEvidence: Identifies aspects of their own position that plausibly affected this study's access, data or interpretation, and omits those that did not
Explains the likely effect of each aspect and the steps taken to address it, such as memoing, member checking or peer debriefing
Uses first-person reference confidently and appropriately to the field
Integrates reflexive comments into methods and discussion where they bear on specific decisions or interpretations
Distinguishes positionality statements from personal narrative or justification of interest in the topic
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two positionality statements, one listing identity categories without consequence and one linking a specific insider position to access and interpretation. Ask which is more useful to a reader and why, then ask for a three-sentence statement for their own study. Check for specificity, stated consequences and actions taken.

topics.name: The academic publishing process
topics.description: Understand the stages through which a manuscript becomes a publication — submission, editorial screening and desk rejection, peer review (single-anonymous, double-anonymous, open), decisions (accept, minor or major revision, reject and resubmit, reject), revision, acceptance, production and post-publication correction or retraction — and the roles of editors, reviewers and authors in each. Understanding the process as a negotiation within a discourse community helps novice authors interpret decisions, plan timelines and avoid treating rejection as a final verdict on their work.
masteryEvidence: Describes the stages of the publication process in their target field, including typical timescales and decision types
Distinguishes the roles and responsibilities of editors, reviewers and authors at each stage
Interprets a decision letter correctly, including what a 'major revision' or 'reject and resubmit' invites the author to do
Identifies field-specific differences, for example conference proceedings in computer science, monographs in the humanities and preprint servers in physics
Explains post-publication processes such as corrections, retractions and open peer review in relation to research integrity
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an anonymised decision letter (major revision) with three reviewer reports. Ask what the editor is asking for, which comments are essential to address and what the realistic next steps and timescale are. Check whether they read the decision as an invitation to revise and distinguish the editor's priorities from individual reviewers' preferences.

topics.name: Selecting a journal
topics.description: Choose a target journal by matching the manuscript's contribution, method and audience to a journal's aims and scope, readership, article types, recent content, review practices, indexing, open-access options and costs, and turnaround, while screening out predatory or deceptive venues. Writers then read and apply the author guidelines and shape the manuscript for that journal's conversation, ideally choosing the journal before drafting rather than after.
masteryEvidence: Produces a shortlist of three journals with a justified ranking based on scope, audience, article type and recent content
Analyses recent issues of a target journal to identify the conversations the manuscript would join
Recognises warning signs of predatory or deceptive journals and verifies indexing and membership claims
Extracts the requirements in author guidelines (length, structure, referencing, data availability, declarations) and applies them to a manuscript
Weighs open-access routes and article processing charges against funder requirements and available support
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a manuscript abstract and three candidate journals, one of them with predatory characteristics. Ask them to rank the journals and justify the ranking in five minutes. Check whether they use scope and recent content rather than prestige alone and whether they detect and explain the problematic venue.

topics.name: Cover letters to editors
topics.description: Write submission letters that identify the manuscript and article type, state concisely what it contributes and why it fits the journal's scope and readership, and make the declarations the journal requires (originality, no simultaneous submission, conflicts of interest, ethics, data availability, suggested or excluded reviewers). The letter is an occluded genre, rarely seen by novices, whose readers are busy editors deciding whether to send a paper for review, so it must be brief, specific and professional.
masteryEvidence: Writes a cover letter of one page or less that names the manuscript, article type and journal
States the contribution and its relevance to the journal's readers in two or three specific sentences, referring to the journal's scope or recent content
Includes all declarations required by the journal's instructions, accurately
Uses a formal, confident register without excessive deference or overclaiming
Avoids pasting the abstract as the body of the letter
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a weak cover letter that pastes the abstract, is effusively deferential and omits a required declaration. Ask them to revise it for a named journal. Check whether the revision states fit and contribution specifically, includes the declaration and adopts a professional register.

topics.name: Responding to reviewers
topics.description: Write response-to-reviewer letters that thank reviewers, address every comment point by point, describe precisely what was changed and where, and explain politely and with evidence when a requested change has not been made. The genre requires managing face, since authors must disagree with gatekeepers while remaining cooperative, as well as clear organisation and consistency between the response and the revised manuscript.
masteryEvidence: Organises a response with each reviewer comment reproduced or summarised, followed by a response and the location of the change
Describes revisions specifically, quoting new text or giving page and line numbers
Declines or partly accepts a requested change with a reasoned, evidence-based and polite explanation
Uses appreciation and mitigation strategically without effusive or formulaic deference
Reconciles conflicting reviewer requests and explains the resolution to the editor
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two reviewer comments, one reasonable and one that misreads the study, and ask for a response to each. Check whether the first is accepted with a precise description of the change, and whether the second is declined or clarified politely, with evidence, without defensiveness and without capitulating to an unjustified request.

topics.name: Writing peer review reports
topics.description: Write reviewer reports for journals or conferences that summarise the manuscript and its claimed contribution, evaluate its significance, methods, evidence and argument, distinguish major from minor issues, make actionable suggestions and give a recommendation consistent with the comments. Reports must be constructive, appropriately mitigated and respectful, and reviewers must meet ethical obligations of confidentiality, competence, timeliness and disclosure of conflicts of interest.
masteryEvidence: Opens with a fair summary of the manuscript's aims, methods, findings and claimed contribution
Separates major concerns that affect the validity of conclusions from minor and presentational points
Phrases criticism as specific, actionable suggestions with reasons, using mitigation without obscuring the point
Gives a recommendation consistent with the severity of the comments
Identifies the ethical obligations of reviewers, including confidentiality and declaring competing interests
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short manuscript extract with one serious methodological flaw and several minor issues, and ask for a 300-word review.
