Check whether the flaw is identified as major and explained, whether minor points are separated, whether the tone is constructive and whether the recommendation matches the comments.

topics.name: Conference abstracts
topics.description: Write abstracts and proposals for conference submission that persuade reviewers of relevance to the conference theme, interest and feasibility, often before the research is complete. Writers adapt the research-abstract moves to a call for papers: framing the topic for the conference audience, stating the aim and approach, reporting results or expected outcomes honestly, and signalling what attendees will gain, within strict word limits and format requirements.
masteryEvidence: Analyses a call for papers and identifies the theme, strands, criteria and format requirements
Writes an abstract within the word limit that links the work to the conference theme and audience
Reports preliminary or expected findings with appropriate tense and hedging, without promising results not yet obtained
Signals the presentation's value to attendees, such as a finding, method, implication or discussion point
Adjusts the abstract for different submission types, such as paper, poster, panel or work in progress
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a call for papers and their research summary (data collection still in progress) and ask for a 250-word abstract. Check whether it connects to the theme, states the aim and approach, handles incomplete results honestly with future or hedged language and signals what the audience will gain.

topics.name: Thesis defence and viva
topics.description: Prepare for and take part in the oral examination of a thesis: understanding the local format and possible outcomes, re-reading the thesis strategically, anticipating questions about contribution, design, findings, limitations and future work, and answering by explaining, defending, conceding and clarifying in extended spoken interaction with expert examiners. Formats vary widely, from closed UK-style vivas with internal and external examiners to public defences with an opponent in parts of continental Europe and committee defences in North America, while in some systems, such as many Australian universities, there is no oral examination.
masteryEvidence: Describes the format, participants, procedures and possible outcomes of the viva or defence in their institution
Summarises the thesis, its contribution and its limitations orally in two to three minutes
Answers challenging questions by clarifying the question, giving a direct answer and supporting it with reference to the thesis
Concedes valid criticisms without abandoning the thesis's main claims and defends choices with reasons
Manages extended interaction, including asking for clarification, taking time to think and navigating to relevant pages
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run a ten-minute mock viva with three questions: one open (summarise your contribution), one challenging (why not method X?) and one about a genuine limitation. Check whether the learner answers directly, supports answers with reference to the thesis, concedes appropriately and maintains the main claims.

topics.name: Authorship and contribution
topics.description: Understand what qualifies someone for authorship, using criteria such as the ICMJE's, and how contributions are described with contributor-role taxonomies such as CRediT, how author order conventions differ across disciplines, and what counts as honorary, guest or ghost authorship. Researchers should be able to discuss authorship early in collaborations, including with supervisors, and to write accurate contribution statements and acknowledgements, including declarations of the use of AI tools, which journals do not accept as authors.
masteryEvidence: Applies a published authorship standard to decide whether a set of described contributions qualifies for authorship or acknowledgement
Writes a contributor statement using CRediT roles for a multi-author paper
Explains author-order conventions in their field and how they differ elsewhere, for example alphabetical order, first and last positions or equal contribution
Identifies honorary, guest and ghost authorship as integrity problems
Opens an authorship conversation with collaborators or supervisors early in a project, using appropriate pragmatic strategies
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a scenario describing five people's contributions to a paper (data collection only, supervision only, analysis and drafting, funding acquisition, critical revision) and ask who should be an author and who should be acknowledged, according to ICMJE. Check whether they apply all the criteria rather than only effort, and whether they note field variation.

topics.name: Publishing as a multilingual scholar
topics.description: Understand the opportunities and inequities of English-medium publishing for multilingual scholars: the dominance of English in high-status indexes, the extra time and cost of writing in an additional language, the material constraints faced by scholars outside well-resourced institutions, reviewer and editor attitudes to non-standard English, and the role of literacy brokers such as co-authors, editors, translators and language professionals. Scholars can use this understanding to make informed choices about language, venue, collaboration and support, and to recognise structural barriers as structural rather than personal failings.
masteryEvidence: Explains how indexing, evaluation systems and journal policies create pressure to publish in English and what this means for research in other languages
Identifies the kinds of literacy brokers available to them and the ethical boundaries of each kind of help
Distinguishes reviewer comments about clarity that need action from comments that reflect native-speaker bias, and responds to each appropriately
Makes a reasoned decision about the language and venue for a particular piece of work, including multilingual dissemination
Draws on their multilingual repertoire as a resource in reading, writing and collaborative networks
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a reviewer comment stating 'the English must be checked by a native speaker' attached to a clear manuscript, and ask how they would respond and what support they might seek. Check whether they separate any genuine clarity issues from bias, respond professionally, and know the legitimate forms of language support and their disclosure requirements.

topics.name: Communicating research beyond academia
topics.description: Communicate research to non-academic audiences such as the public, practitioners, policymakers and industry through lay summaries, blogs, social media, talks, visual summaries and impact case material, adapting content, structure, register and claims to each audience while keeping them accurate. Researchers also plan engagement deliberately, as many funders and evaluation systems expect, and manage the risks of oversimplification and online visibility.
masteryEvidence: Writes a lay summary of their research that a non-specialist reader can restate accurately
Adapts the same finding for two different audiences, such as practitioners and the general public, changing framing, detail and register
Preserves the calibration of claims when simplifying, avoiding causal or certainty inflation
Plans an engagement activity with a stated audience, purpose, channel and indicator of reach or benefit
Manages an online professional presence, such as a profile or social media, in line with institutional guidance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a 150-word lay summary of a hedged research finding from their own work, then have a non-specialist peer restate it. Check whether the restatement is accurate, whether jargon has been removed or explained, and whether the hedging of the original claim has survived simplification.

topics.name: Academic CVs, biographies and personal statements
topics.description: Write the self-presentation genres of academic careers: academic CVs, with conventional sections, consistent referencing of outputs and evidence of research, teaching and service; short biographical statements for conferences, journals and profiles, often in the third person; and personal statements for postgraduate study, scholarships and posts, which must show fit, motivation and capability with evidence. Each genre balances self-promotion with modesty according to its conventions, and conventions differ across countries and sectors.
masteryEvidence: Organises an academic CV with conventional sections in a sensible order for the target post and formats publications consistently
Writes a 100-word third-person bio that foregrounds current role, research focus and relevant achievements
Writes a personal statement that addresses the stated criteria with specific evidence rather than general enthusiasm
Adjusts the degree of self-promotion and personal information to the genre and the national or institutional context
Describes their own contributions to co-authored or collaborative work accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a personal statement full of general claims ('I have always been passionate about…') and the selection criteria for a postgraduate programme. Ask them to revise two paragraphs. Check whether the revision addresses the criteria with specific evidence and adopts an appropriately confident register.

topics.name: Types of visuals and their functions
topics.description: Recognise the main visual forms in academic texts (line graphs, bar charts, pie charts, scatterplots, tables, flowcharts, diagrams, maps and photographs) and the relationship each is designed to show: change over time, comparison between categories, part–whole composition, distribution, association between variables, sequence or spatial layout. Knowing what a visual is for guides how it is read and which language is needed to describe it.
masteryEvidence: Names common visual types and matches each to the relationship it typically represents (trend, comparison, composition, distribution, association, process, location)
Explains why a given dataset is better shown as a table than a graph, or as a line graph than a pie chart
Identifies visuals whose type is mismatched to their data, such as a line joining unordered categories or a pie chart of non-exclusive responses
Distinguishes data displays (graphs, tables) from conceptual visuals (models, flowcharts, photographs) and predicts the different commentary each invites
topics.assessmentPrompt: Describe four small datasets in words (monthly temperatures over two years; market share of five firms; height and weight of 40 students; twelve exact values a reader must look up) and ask which visual suits each and why. Check that choices follow the relationship in the data (time → line graph; part–whole → pie or stacked bar; association → scatterplot; look-up → table) and are justified by function rather than appearance.

topics.name: Reading graphs and charts
topics.description: Read graphs and charts systematically: check the title, axes, scales, units, legend and source before interpreting; then extract values, compare across series, and identify the overall pattern, exceptions and notable features. Accurate reading at the levels of individual data, relationships between data and inferences beyond the data underpins both data commentary and critical evaluation of others’ visuals.
masteryEvidence: Checks title, axis labels, units, scale intervals and legend before interpreting any values
Reads specific values accurately, including from logarithmic, dual or non-zero-based axes
Identifies the overall pattern and the most important exceptions, peaks, crossovers or outliers
Distinguishes what the graph shows directly from inferences or predictions beyond the plotted data
Notes missing information that limits interpretation, such as absent units, sample size or source
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a two-series line graph whose y-axis starts at 40 and whose final point is marked as an estimate. Ask one read-off question, one comparison between the series and one ‘what might explain this / what would you expect next’ question. Check read-off accuracy, correct units in the comparison, whether the learner notices the truncated axis and the estimate, and whether the inference is marked as tentative.

topics.name: Reading tables
topics.description: Navigate tables by identifying what rows and columns represent, the units, totals, notes, abbreviations and significance markers; locate specific values; and compare across rows or columns to identify the main pattern. Research articles often carry findings in tables that the prose mentions only briefly, so efficient table reading is essential for accurate source use.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the variables in rows and columns, the units and any totals or subtotals
Uses table notes, footnote symbols and abbreviations (n, M, SD, asterisks for significance) to interpret entries
Locates specific values quickly and compares across rows and columns accurately
States the most important pattern or difference in a table and points to the cells that show it
Checks claims in the prose against the table and notices discrepancies or overstatement
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a results table from a research article (means, standard deviations, sample sizes and a significance asterisk) together with the article’s one-sentence summary of it. Ask the learner to find two specific values, state the main pattern and judge whether the summary sentence represents the table accurately. Check correct use of the notes and whether any overstatement in the summary is noticed.

topics.name: Describing trends and change
topics.description: Describe change over time precisely using verbs (rise, fall, fluctuate, level off, peak), nouns (an increase in, a decline of), degree and speed modifiers (slightly, sharply, a gradual rise), prepositions of quantity and time (from … to, by, at, over the period) and appropriate tense. Precise trend language lets writers summarise patterns economically and select only the changes that matter to their point.
masteryEvidence: Uses verb and noun patterns for change with accurate prepositions (rose by five points to 20%; an increase of 5% in output)
Chooses degree and speed modifiers proportionate to the size of the change and the scale of the graph, rather than defaulting to dramatic intensifiers
Selects tense appropriately: past for completed periods, present for what the figure shows, modal or future forms for projections
States an overall trend before detail and groups similar changes
Varies structures (verb, nominal, there was) without loss of precision
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a line graph with three series over ten years, including one small change, one sharp change and one plateau. Ask for a 100-word description. Check preposition accuracy (by/to/from/of/in), whether modifiers are proportionate (a two-point change is not ‘dramatic’), whether an overall trend precedes detail, and tense consistency.

topics.name: Describing proportions and comparisons
topics.description: Express proportions and comparisons in data precisely, using fractions, percentages, ratios and multiples (a third of, 42% of, a ratio of 3:1, twice as many as), quantifiers (the majority, a substantial minority, nearly all) and comparative and superlative structures with numbers. This allows exact, checkable comparisons between groups and categories rather than vague impressions.
masteryEvidence: Expresses proportions with accurate articles, prepositions and agreement (a third of respondents were; the proportion of graduates was)
Uses comparative and multiplicative structures with numbers accurately (twice as likely as; 15 percentage points higher than; the largest share)
Matches quantifiers (most, the majority, a substantial minority) to the actual proportions they describe
Chooses between percentage, fraction and ratio according to which makes the comparison clearest for the reader
Avoids or clarifies ambiguous multiplicative comparisons such as three times more than
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a pie chart and a grouped bar chart of survey responses from two groups. Ask for five sentences comparing the groups. Check agreement after proportion/percentage/fraction phrases, comparative grammar with numbers, whether quantifiers fit the values (is 52% ‘the vast majority’?) and whether at least one sentence compares between groups rather than within one.

topics.name: Data commentary
topics.description: Write commentary that uses data as evidence: locate the visual and summarise what it shows, highlight the findings that matter for the writer’s purpose, and interpret them by explaining, comparing with expectations or previous studies, acknowledging limitations and drawing implications whose strength matches the evidence. Data commentary is the core of results and discussion writing across disciplines and differs from description-only tasks such as IELTS Writing Task 1.
masteryEvidence: Opens with a location statement or summary that links the visual to the purpose of the text
Selects and highlights the two or three findings that matter for the argument rather than describing everything
Offers explanations or implications and calibrates their strength with hedges, approximators and qualifications
Distinguishes association from causation and acknowledges alternative explanations or data limitations
Organises commentary from general to specific and relates it to research questions, expectations or prior studies
Explains how a commentary differs from a test-style description of the same visual
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a figure plus a one-line research question and ask for a 150-word commentary. Check for a location or summary statement; selection of findings relevant to the question; at least one interpretive move (explanation, comparison with expectation or literature, implication); appropriate hedging, with no causal claim drawn from correlational data; and the absence of exhaustive description.

topics.name: Describing processes, diagrams and maps
topics.description: Verbalise non-numerical visuals: the stages, branches and loops of processes and cycles in flowcharts; the components and spatial relations in diagrams of structures and systems; and spatial change shown in maps and plans. This draws on sequencing language, voice choice, purpose and result expressions and locative prepositions, and supports explaining scientific, technical and planning visuals in reports, examinations and presentations.
masteryEvidence: Describes a process or cycle in logical order, including decision branches and loops (if … otherwise; the cycle then repeats)
Chooses passive or active voice according to whether the process or the agent is in focus
Describes spatial relations and changes on maps or plans accurately (to the north of, adjacent to, was replaced by, was extended)
Opens with an overview of the whole process or layout before detail
Groups stages into phases rather than enumerating each step mechanically
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a flowchart with one decision branch and one loop (for example a manuscript review process). Ask for a 120-word description. Check that the overview states the start, end and number of main phases, that the branch and loop are expressed accurately, and that voice choices follow focus.

topics.name: Figure and table captions
topics.description: Number, title and caption figures and tables according to the required style, write informative titles and notes that let the visual stand alone, define abbreviations, symbols and units, and acknowledge the source of reproduced or adapted visuals. Correct labelling makes visuals referable in the text and, when visuals or data come from others, is part of academic integrity.
masteryEvidence: Numbers tables and figures in separate sequences in order of first mention
Writes concise, informative titles that state what is shown, for whom or where, and when
Adds notes defining abbreviations, symbols and units so the visual can be understood without the main text
Attributes reproduced or adapted visuals and data using the required wording (e.g., Adapted from; Data from) with a matching reference-list entry
Follows the placement and formatting conventions of the required style guide or journal
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a figure adapted from a published source with a vague title (‘Graph 1’) and undefined abbreviations. Ask the learner to rewrite the number, title, notes and attribution in the course style. Check numbering, informativeness of the title, definition of abbreviations, attribution wording and a matching reference-list entry.

topics.name: Creating effective visuals
topics.description: Choose the visual form that best serves a message and audience, and design it for clarity and honesty: an appropriate chart type, honest scales and baselines, minimal non-data decoration, direct labelling, accessible colour and enough context (units, sample size, uncertainty). Well-designed visuals let readers check claims quickly and are increasingly assessed in reports, posters and theses.
masteryEvidence: Selects a chart type that matches the relationship to be shown and the audience, and justifies the choice
Sets scales, baselines and aspect ratios that represent the data without exaggerating or concealing differences
Removes non-essential decoration (3D effects, heavy gridlines, redundant legends) and labels data directly where possible
Uses colour purposefully and accessibly, without relying on colour alone to distinguish series
Includes units, sample sizes and, where relevant, indicators of uncertainty such as error bars or confidence intervals
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a cluttered spreadsheet-default chart (e.g., a 3D pie chart or a bar chart with a distant legend) and its data. Ask them to redesign it for a stated message and audience and annotate three changes. Check that each change is justified by the message, honesty or accessibility (type, scale, labelling, colour) rather than by appearance alone.

topics.name: Recognising misleading visuals
topics.description: Recognise design and data choices that distort a visual’s message (truncated or inconsistent axes, selective time windows, dual axes, area and 3D distortion, mismatched chart types, missing denominators or uncertainty) and judge whether conclusions drawn from the visual are justified. This is a component of statistical literacy and of the critical evaluation of sources.
masteryEvidence: Identifies truncated, inconsistent or dual axes and explains how they change perceived magnitude
Detects selective time windows and omitted comparison groups
Recognises area, volume and 3D effects that misrepresent proportions
Asks for missing context (denominators, sample size, uncertainty, data source) before accepting a visual claim
Distinguishes deliberate or careless distortion from defensible conventions, such as a non-zero baseline on a line graph of small variations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show two versions of the same data (one with a truncated y-axis and a narrow time window, one complete) with a headline claim. Ask whether the headline is justified. Check that the learner names the specific design choices, explains their effect, asks about the data source or denominator, and does not dismiss every non-zero baseline as dishonest.

topics.name: Referring to visuals in text
topics.description: Integrate visuals into prose by referring to them explicitly and purposefully (Figure 2 shows; as shown in Table 1; see Figure 3), placing references where the reader needs them, choosing verbs that suit visual subjects and the strength of the claim (show, indicate, illustrate, suggest), and telling the reader what to notice. This links visual evidence to the argument instead of leaving visuals to speak for themselves.
masteryEvidence: Refers to every visual in the text by number, at or before the point where it appears
Uses a range of integration structures (visual as subject, as-clauses, parenthetical references) grammatically, avoiding blends such as as Figure 2 shows that
Chooses verbs with visual subjects that match the claim (shows vs suggests vs illustrates)
Tells the reader what to notice rather than merely pointing to the visual
Avoids duplicating in the text every value already shown in the visual
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph in which three figures are referred to poorly (no number, ‘the following graph’, a reference after the visual, ‘as Table 1 shows that’). Ask the learner to revise it. Check for numbered references, grammatical as-clauses, a statement of what to notice, and removal of duplicated values.

topics.name: Expressing quantities accurately
topics.description: Express numbers, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios and rates accurately in prose, together with the grammar around them: articles and of-phrases (a third of, two-thirds of the sample), agreement (a quarter of respondents were), per cent versus percentage, number of versus amount of, rates (per capita, per 1,000) and multiplicative forms. Accurate quantity expressions are the basis of every claim made from data.
masteryEvidence: Reads aloud and writes fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios and large numbers correctly in words and figures
Uses partitive and quantity structures with accurate articles, prepositions and agreement
Distinguishes per cent (with a number) from percentage (a proportion), and number of from amount of
Expresses rates and ratios unambiguously (per 1,000 population; a ratio of 3:2; one in five)
Converts between equivalent forms (0.25, 25%, a quarter, one in four) to suit the reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present ten quantities in mixed forms (0.05, 3/8, 1:4, 12.5%, 2.3 million, 4 per 1,000) and ask the learner to use each in a full sentence about a sample. Check partitive structures and agreement, the per cent/percentage distinction, and the expression of decimals and large numbers.

topics.name: Approximation and precision
topics.description: Approximate and round quantities appropriately (approximately, roughly, just under, well over, in the region of, nearly a third, an estimated) and decide when exact figures or approximation better serve the reader and purpose. Approximators also function as hedges: they signal the writer’s commitment to exactness and must be consistent with the figures and with the precision of the measurement.
masteryEvidence: Uses approximators and boundary expressions accurately (just under, just over, nearly, slightly more than, in excess of)
Rounds figures to a precision consistent with the measurement and sample (e.g., not reporting 33.33% for three cases)
Chooses between exact and approximate expression according to audience and genre (results section vs lay summary)
Keeps approximate verbal expressions consistent with the figures cited alongside them
Avoids both false precision and unnecessary vagueness
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a small table of exact values and ask for two short summaries: one for a results section and one for a lay summary. Check that the results version gives appropriately rounded figures, the lay version uses approximators accurately (‘just under half’ for 47%, not for 41%), and neither introduces false precision.

topics.name: Basic statistical vocabulary
topics.description: Understand and use core statistical terms accurately in reading and writing: population and sample, variable, mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation, distribution, correlation, outlier, significance, error and bias. Several of these words have everyday meanings that differ from their technical sense (significant, normal, error, random, confidence, bias), so precise use is essential for credible methods and results writing.
masteryEvidence: Defines core descriptive and inferential terms accurately in plain English
Distinguishes everyday from statistical senses of significant, random, error, bias, normal and confidence
Uses the terms with conventional collocation and grammar (a strong positive correlation between X and Y; statistically significant at the .05 level; normally distributed)
Chooses between mean and median when summarising skewed data and explains the choice
Recognises common symbols and abbreviations (M, SD, n, N, r, p, CI) in texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sentences mixing everyday and statistical senses (e.g., ‘There was a significant number of complaints’; ‘The difference was significant, p = .03’). Ask the learner to label each sense and rewrite any ambiguous sentence for a quantitative report. Check that statistical significance is distinguished from importance and that ‘significant’ is not used without a test.

topics.name: Interpreting statistical claims
topics.description: Read and interpret inferential statistics at an informed consumer level: understand what p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes do and do not indicate, distinguish statistical significance from practical importance, and recognise how sample size and design limit conclusions. This allows learners to evaluate quantitative sources and report them accurately without overstating them.
masteryEvidence: Explains in plain English what a p-value does and does not indicate, avoiding the reading that it is the probability that a hypothesis is true
Distinguishes statistical significance from the size and practical importance of an effect
Interprets a confidence interval as a range of values compatible with the data and comments on its width
Recognises when a non-significant result is misreported as evidence of no effect
Reports a quantitative finding from a source with appropriate hedging, effect-size information and reference to design
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an abstract reporting ‘a significant effect (p = .04)’ from a large sample with a small effect size, together with a news headline calling it ‘a major breakthrough’. Ask the learner to judge the headline and rewrite it. Check whether they separate significance from size, mention sample size or design, and avoid both overclaiming and dismissing the finding.

topics.name: Relative and absolute change
topics.description: Distinguish relative from absolute change (per cent versus percentage points; relative versus absolute risk; rates versus counts) and choose and interpret framings that do not mislead. The same result can be presented as ‘a 50% reduction’ or as ‘a fall from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000’, and readers and writers need to recognise how framing shapes judgement.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes a change in percentage points from a percentage change and calculates both from the same data
Converts a relative risk reduction into an absolute risk reduction when given a baseline
Identifies sources that report only relative figures and explains why this may mislead
Chooses transparent framings (absolute figures, natural frequencies) when writing for non-specialist readers
Distinguishes counts from rates and notices missing denominators
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present ‘Unemployment rose from 4% to 5%’ and ask the learner to express the change in percentage points and as a percentage change, and to say which a newspaper might choose and why. Then give ‘a treatment halves the risk of X’ with a baseline of 2 in 1,000 and ask for an absolute statement. Check the calculations and the explanation of framing effects.

topics.name: Units and measurement
topics.description: Report measurements using SI units and symbols correctly (symbols versus names, a space between number and unit, prefixes, no plural or full stop on symbols, compound units such as m/s or kg m⁻³) and follow discipline and style-guide conventions where these differ. Correct use of units is a precondition for credibility and replicability in science, engineering and health writing.
masteryEvidence: Writes unit symbols and prefixes with correct case (mg, kHz, μm, mL or ml) and without plural or full-stop forms (not kgs or cm.)
Separates number and unit symbol with a space, following any style-guide exceptions consistently
Expresses compound units in one consistent format
Says measurements aloud in a form consistent with the written symbol (‘five milligrams per litre’)
Keeps units and their formatting consistent across text, tables and figures
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short methods paragraph containing eight unit errors (e.g., 5Kg, 20 mins., 3 mls, inconsistent 37°C and 37 °C, m/s/s). Ask the learner to correct it with reference to an SI summary and the course style guide. Check symbol case, spacing, plurals, compound units and internal consistency.

topics.name: Language of mathematical expression
topics.description: Read and write mathematical expressions in academic prose: verbalising equations and inequalities, introducing and defining variables (where x denotes; let n be), integrating displayed equations into sentences with appropriate punctuation, and using conventional phrasing for relationships (is proportional to, tends to, is a function of). This is needed wherever formulae carry the argument, as in science, engineering, economics and quantitative social science.
masteryEvidence: Reads equations, inequalities and common notation aloud accurately, including grouping (the square of x plus y vs x plus y, all squared)
Defines every variable and parameter on first use, typically with a where-clause
Integrates displayed equations into sentences grammatically, with appropriate punctuation
Uses conventional verbal formulations for relationships (is directly proportional to, increases linearly with, is inversely related to)
Distinguishes italic quantity symbols from upright unit symbols and function names
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a displayed formula from the learner’s discipline (e.g., a regression equation or a kinematic formula). Ask the learner to read it aloud and to write the sentence that introduces it and defines its terms. Check accuracy of verbalisation including grouping, a where-clause defining all variables, punctuation around the display, and conventional relational verbs.

topics.name: Multimodal literacy
topics.description: Understand how image, layout, colour, typography and text combine to make meaning, and analyse how a multimodal text directs attention through salience, reading path, framing and the placement of information. This awareness underpins both critical reading of academic multimodal texts and the design of posters, slides and digital assignments.
masteryEvidence: Describes how layout, salience and framing guide a reader’s path through a poster, slide or web page
Explains the division of labour between image and text in an academic visual, stating what each conveys that the other does not
Uses a basic metalanguage of visual design (salience, framing, reading path, information value) to analyse examples
Identifies disciplinary conventions in visual communication, such as the visual types typical of conference talks in their field
Critiques a multimodal text for coherence between its modes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a research poster or infographic for 30 seconds, then hide it. Ask what the learner noticed first, second and third. Show it again and ask which design features (size, position, colour, framing) produced that order. Check for use of design concepts beyond ‘it looks nice’ and for recognition of how image and text share the message.

topics.name: Designing academic posters
topics.description: Design an academic poster that communicates a clear main message at a glance and supports conversation in a poster session: a hierarchy of title, key finding and supporting sections; a logical reading path; economical text; visuals that carry the evidence; and legibility at viewing distance. The poster is a genre with its own norms, not a shrunken paper.
masteryEvidence: States the poster’s main message in a headline or prominently placed key finding
Organises sections along a clear reading path using columns, numbering or visual flow
Reduces text to essential claims within a word budget, using phrases and lists where appropriate
Uses visuals as the primary evidence, each with an informative caption
Ensures legibility (type size, contrast) and accessible design at the intended viewing distance
Explains design decisions in relation to the audience and the session format
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a text-heavy draft poster (around 1,200 words in abstract-style paragraphs). Ask them to identify three problems and propose a redesign plan with a word budget and a headline finding. Check that they prioritise the main message, cut text, convert prose results into visuals where possible, and attend to reading path and legibility.

topics.name: Infographics and visual summaries
topics.description: Condense information into visual summaries (infographics, visual abstracts and one-page summaries) for academic and public audiences: select the essential message, structure it visually, and preserve accuracy, attribution and appropriate qualification. Visual summaries are increasingly used in assessment and research dissemination, and they risk oversimplification when impact is pursued at the expense of accuracy.
masteryEvidence: Selects one core message and a small number of supporting points for the summary
Structures content with a clear visual hierarchy and reading path
Preserves the accuracy and essential qualifications of claims when simplifying
Represents numbers honestly and in formats suited to the audience
Attributes data and images and includes the source reference
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a research abstract and ask the learner to sketch, in 20 minutes, a visual abstract or infographic for a public audience. Check that the core finding is accurate and appropriately qualified, the structure is clear, numbers are represented honestly and in an accessible format, and the source is cited.

topics.name: Video essays and digital assessments
topics.description: Produce assessed multimodal genres (podcasts, video essays, narrated presentations, e-portfolios and websites), understanding their purposes, criteria and conventions, and orchestrating speech, text, image and sound to build an academic argument with appropriate attribution of sources and media. These genres keep the core academic expectations of argument, evidence and citation while changing the means of expression.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the purpose, audience and assessment criteria of a digital assignment, including the academic expectations that still apply
Plans with a script or storyboard showing how the modes are coordinated to build an argument
Integrates and attributes sources, images, music and footage in ways suited to the medium
Uses a spoken register and pacing suited to recorded academic delivery
Provides accessibility features such as captions or transcripts where required
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a brief for a five-minute video essay and ask the learner to storyboard the first minute with script excerpts and source attributions. Check that the argument is explicit, the modes complement rather than duplicate one another, sources and media are attributed, and captions or a transcript are planned.

topics.name: Accessible academic documents
topics.description: Produce documents, slides and media that are accessible to readers with disabilities and to assistive technologies: structured headings created with styles, meaningful alternative text for images and charts, sufficient colour contrast, meaning not conveyed by colour alone, descriptive link text, readable typography, and captions or transcripts for audio-visual content. Accessibility is an institutional and often legal expectation, and it improves clarity for all readers.
masteryEvidence: Applies heading styles and a logical reading order rather than relying on visual formatting
Writes alternative text that conveys the purpose and key message of an image or chart, and provides a longer description for complex visuals
Checks colour contrast and avoids relying on colour alone to convey meaning
Uses descriptive link text and table structures that assistive technologies can interpret
Provides captions or transcripts for recorded audio-visual work
Runs an accessibility checker and interprets its results critically, recognising what it cannot judge
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short document containing a chart, a decorative image, colour-coded text and ‘click here’ links. Ask the learner to make it accessible and explain each change. Check heading structure, quality of alternative text (key message rather than ‘graph of data’), handling of the decorative image, colour-independent meaning and descriptive links.

topics.name: Self-regulated learning
topics.description: Understand self-regulated learning as a cyclical process of forethought (analysing the task, setting goals, planning strategies, appraising one's self-efficacy), performance (self-monitoring and controlled strategy use) and self-reflection (evaluating outcomes against standards, attributing causes and adapting). The model gives learners and teachers a shared language for locating where independent study breaks down.
masteryEvidence: Describes the three phases of a self-regulation cycle and the main processes in each, using an example from their own study

Analyses a recent assignment or test experience and locates the main breakdown in a specific phase (for example, no analysis of the brief, no monitoring during drafting, no use of feedback afterwards)
Attributes outcomes to controllable factors such as strategy choice and preparation rather than to fixed ability or luck
Proposes a specific adjustment for the next cycle that follows logically from their self-evaluation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short case of a student who spent many hours on an essay and received a low mark with comments on structure and relevance. Ask the learner what went wrong in each phase and what the student should do next time. Look for phase-specific diagnosis (for example, no analysis of the question or criteria at forethought) and controllable attributions, rather than 'work harder'.

topics.name: Setting language and academic goals
topics.description: Set specific, near-term and checkable language and academic goals derived from actual course and assessment demands, and turn them into planned actions, including if–then plans for predictable obstacles. Well-formed goals turn a general wish to 'improve my English' into decisions about what to practise this week and how progress will be judged.
masteryEvidence: Writes goals that specify the skill or language feature, the context of use, a success indicator and a time frame
Derives goals from evidence (feedback, marking criteria, diagnostic results, programme requirements) rather than general impressions
Breaks a distant goal, such as meeting a progression requirement, into near-term sub-goals with dates
Pairs goals with if–then plans for anticipated obstacles
Reviews and revises goals at planned intervals in the light of progress evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner their latest written feedback and ask them to set two goals for the next fortnight. Check whether each goal is traceable to the feedback, specific enough that progress could be checked, and paired with a concrete action and time; 'improve my academic vocabulary' with no action or indicator is a gap response.

topics.name: Time and workload management
topics.description: Plan, prioritise and protect study time across concurrent deadlines: estimating task duration realistically, scheduling backwards from deadlines, allocating time to independent study as well as taught sessions, and recognising and countering procrastination. For L2 learners, realistic estimates must include the extra time that reading and writing in English may take.
masteryEvidence: Produces a weekly plan that includes taught sessions, scheduled independent study blocks and deadlines across modules
Plans backwards from a deadline, breaking a task into dated stages such as reading, planning, drafting and revising, with buffer time
Compares estimated and actual task durations and adjusts future estimates accordingly
Prioritises tasks by deadline, weighting and dependency rather than by preference or ease
Identifies personal procrastination triggers and applies a specific countermeasure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a two-week scenario with three overlapping deliverables of different weightings and ask for a schedule. Check for backward planning, prioritisation by weighting and dependency, buffer time and realistic durations; scheduling most work for the final days or ignoring weighting indicates a gap.

topics.name: Independent study
topics.description: Understand the scale and purpose of independent study in higher education systems where expected study hours far exceed contact hours (in many UK institutions one credit conventionally represents about ten notional learning hours), and plan that time productively: preparing for and consolidating taught sessions, following up reading, practising language and progressing assessments without waiting for instructions.
masteryEvidence: Estimates the independent study a module expects from its credit value or handbook and compares this with their current practice
Plans independent study that includes preparation before, and consolidation after, specific taught sessions
Selects independent study activities that address identified needs rather than repeating class activities
Records what independent study was done and its outcome in a form that can be reviewed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a module handbook page giving credit value and contact hours. Ask how many hours of independent study per week this implies and what they will do in those hours next week. Look for a realistic estimate and activities tied to particular sessions and assessments rather than 'revise' or 'read more'.

topics.name: Evidence-based study techniques
topics.description: Choose and use study techniques that cognitive research rates highly for durable learning (above all retrieval practice and distributed practice, with interleaving and self-explanation as promising options) instead of relying on lower-utility habits such as rereading, highlighting and copying notes. The techniques apply to language items (vocabulary, formulaic phrases, citation conventions) as well as disciplinary content.
masteryEvidence: Converts notes or readings into retrieval questions and self-tests without looking at the source
Schedules several spaced reviews of the same material rather than one massed session
Explains why rereading and highlighting create a sense of familiarity that overestimates learning
Applies retrieval and spacing to language items such as academic collocations and reporting verbs, not only to content
Mixes question or problem types in practice when the assessment will require choosing between methods
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show how they would prepare for a quiz on a lecture they attended last week, using their own notes. Look for self-testing (cover-and-recall, questions, flashcards) and a spaced schedule; a plan built on rereading and highlighting, or a single long session the night before, indicates a gap.

topics.name: Learner autonomy
topics.description: Understand learner autonomy as a developing capacity to take control over one's learning (choosing objectives, content and methods, and monitoring and evaluating progress) that grows through supported practice, rather than as studying alone or without a teacher. Autonomy underpins the independent study, strategy choice and continued development that universities expect but rarely teach explicitly.
masteryEvidence: Explains the difference between autonomy as control over learning decisions and isolation or unsupported self-instruction
Makes and justifies a learning decision that no teacher has prescribed, such as selecting additional materials for a known weakness
Evaluates the outcome of a self-initiated learning activity and decides whether to continue, adapt or abandon it
Identifies constraints on their control in a given context (assessment rules, time, resources) and works within or around them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask: 'Describe something you learned in English in the last fortnight that no teacher asked you to learn. How did you choose it, how did you go about it, and how did you know whether it worked?' A strong answer shows a self-made decision at each stage; a weak one describes only teacher-set work or an intention without action.

topics.name: Language learning strategies
topics.description: Select, combine and evaluate strategies for continuing to develop academic English beyond the course: for example, noticing and recording useful language from disciplinary reading, deliberate vocabulary study, seeking opportunities for spoken interaction and feedback, using the L1 as a resource, and managing affect. Strategies are chosen to fit the task and goal rather than out of habit.
masteryEvidence: Names and uses strategies from several categories (memory, cognitive, compensation, metacognitive, affective, social) that fit an identified need
Combines a cluster of strategies for a specific target, such as noticing, recording and retrieving reporting verbs from set readings
Evaluates whether a strategy is working, using evidence, and replaces those that are not
Creates opportunities outside class for language use and feedback (study groups, office hours, extensive reading or listening in the discipline)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to choose one area to improve (for example, following seminar discussion) and to describe the strategies they will use over a month and how they will know whether they are working. Look for a coherent cluster of strategies matched to the target, including monitoring; a list of generic tips ('watch films', 'read more') with no evaluation indicates a gap.

topics.name: Reflective learning logs
topics.description: Keep a structured learning log or journal that records goals, actions taken, evidence of progress and next steps, and use it to make decisions. The key distinction is between analytical reflection, which explains and leads to action, and description of activities or feelings alone.
masteryEvidence: Writes entries that link a learning action to evidence of its effect and a decision about what to do next
Moves beyond description ('Today I read an article') to analysis ('I followed the method section but not the discussion because…')
Reviews earlier entries to identify patterns across weeks and revises goals accordingly
Uses evidence from the log to support a tutorial conversation or an end-of-course reflection
topics.assessmentPrompt: Take three consecutive entries from the learner's log and ask them to summarise what changed in their learning over that period and why. Look for patterns supported by evidence and decisions that follow from them; if the learner cannot draw anything from the entries, the log is functioning as a diary rather than a learning tool.

topics.name: Using academic support services
topics.description: Identify the academic and personal support a university offers (library and subject librarians, writing or academic skills centres, in-sessional EAP, maths and statistics support, disability, wellbeing and advice services) and use it early, with a prepared and specific request, as a normal part of good study practice rather than a last resort.
masteryEvidence: Locates the right service for a given need (statistics help, a reading-list query, a disability adjustment) using institutional web pages or the VLE
Books and prepares for an appointment with a specific question and the relevant materials (draft, brief, feedback)
Distinguishes what a writing or language support service will and will not do, for example advising on a draft but not proofreading it
Seeks support before a deadline becomes a crisis and records what was learned
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three short scenarios (difficulty interpreting statistical output, a lecturer's comment about 'paragraph structure', anxiety that is disrupting sleep before exams) and ask which service the learner would approach, how, and what they would bring. Check for accurate matching, a specific request and awareness of each service's limits.

topics.name: Sustainable study habits and wellbeing
topics.description: Sustain study across a term or degree by anticipating workload peaks, protecting sleep, breaks and social connection, recognising early signs that stress is affecting learning, and knowing when and how to seek help. Wellbeing is treated here as a condition for learning, not as a clinical intervention.
masteryEvidence: Identifies predictable pressure points in their term (assessment clusters, exam season) and plans for them in advance
Maintains routines for sleep and breaks during assessment periods instead of sacrificing them to extend study hours
Recognises personal early-warning signs (avoidance, disrupted sleep, withdrawal from others) and names an action for each
Matches different levels of concern to appropriate institutional or external services, including urgent routes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to map the next six weeks, marking deadlines and exams, and to note where pressure will peak and what they will do before and during those peaks. Look for anticipation and specific protective actions (earlier starts, reduced commitments, maintained sleep, contact with support) rather than a plan simply to 'work harder'.

topics.name: Motivation and the L2 self
topics.description: Understand motivation for continued language and academic development through Dörnyei's L2 Motivational Self System (the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self and the learning experience), and use a specific, plausible image of oneself as a competent academic user of English, linked to concrete current actions, to sustain effort beyond an entry requirement or the end of an EAP course.
masteryEvidence: Articulates a specific future academic or professional self that uses English (for example, contributing in lab meetings or writing a dissertation) rather than a generic aim to 'improve my English'
Distinguishes goals they hold for themselves from obligations set by others (entry scores, sponsor or family expectations) and explains how each affects their effort
Links their future-self image to at least two concrete learning actions they are taking now
Identifies features of the current learning experience that support or undermine their motivation and proposes a response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write three sentences: who they want to be as a user of English in two years, what they must do this month to move towards that, and what will happen if they do nothing. Check specificity, plausibility and the link between vision and action; a vivid image with no linked action, or an action list with no personal purpose, indicates partial understanding.

topics.name: Metacognitive knowledge
topics.description: Knowledge of oneself as a learner and user of English, of what particular academic tasks demand, and of which strategies suit which tasks and conditions (Flavell's person, task and strategy variables). Accurate metacognitive knowledge allows learners to plan, monitor and adjust their learning rather than relying on habit or on how familiar material feels.
masteryEvidence: Describes their current strengths and gaps across reading, listening, writing and speaking using specific evidence (marks, feedback comments, recurring errors) rather than global labels
Explains how two academic tasks differ in their demands (for example, a source-based coursework essay and a timed short-answer exam) and what that implies for preparation
Names strategies suited to a stated purpose and explains why a familiar strategy such as rereading can create a feeling of knowing without durable learning
Distinguishes a judgement of learning based on familiarity or fluency from one based on a self-test result
Revises a prediction about their own performance after comparing it with the actual outcome
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to predict their score on a short unseen retrieval quiz covering last week's material, take it without notes, then explain any gap between prediction and result and what they would change. Look for explanations framed in terms of task, strategy and self rather than effort or luck alone, and for recognition that familiarity is a weak signal of learning.

topics.name: Learning subject content through English
topics.description: Understand that in foundation, English-medium and degree contexts, disciplinary concepts and the English used to express them are learned together: technical terms, characteristic text types and ways of explaining are part of the content. Learners use this understanding to plan for the double load, for example by previewing terminology, using L1 resources strategically and checking conceptual understanding as well as language.
masteryEvidence: Identifies terms and constructions in a subject text or lecture whose meaning is disciplinary rather than everyday
Distinguishes a comprehension problem caused by the language from one caused by an unfamiliar concept, and applies a different repair to each
Uses L1 or bilingual resources to secure a concept, then re-expresses it in English using the discipline's terms
Explains a disciplinary concept in English at two levels, technical and plain, showing control of both content and language
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short subject-textbook passage containing one sub-technical term (for example 'significant' in a statistics context) and one new concept. Ask the learner to explain the passage, then say which parts were difficult because of the English and which because of the idea. Look for an accurate distinction and a suitable repair strategy for each.

topics.name: University assessment literacy
topics.description: Understand how university assessment works: the difference between formative and summative assessment; how learning outcomes, assessment briefs and marking criteria relate; the range of assessment types; and the rules on weighting, deadlines, word limits, extensions, mitigating circumstances and resits. This knowledge lets learners focus effort where it counts and recognise formative opportunities that carry no marks.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the formative from the summative tasks in a module and explains how to use each
Traces a stated learning outcome to the assessment task and criteria that measure it
Extracts weighting, deadline, word-limit and submission rules accurately from a module handbook or brief
Explains in general terms the procedures for extensions, mitigating circumstances and resits, and identifies where to check the specific rules
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an authentic module handbook extract and ask which tasks count towards the final mark and by how much, which learning outcome each task assesses, and what happens if a deadline is missed. Check for accurate extraction and an explanation of why the formative task matters even though it carries no marks.

topics.name: Interpreting marking criteria
topics.description: Unpack the marking criteria, rubrics and grade descriptors for a specific task: identify what each criterion values, how adjacent bands differ, and what evaluative language such as 'critical', 'well-structured' or 'appropriate use of sources' means in observable textual terms, using exemplars to make tacit standards concrete.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites each criterion in a rubric as a concrete question that can be asked of a draft
Identifies the words that distinguish adjacent bands (for example 'some', 'consistent', 'sophisticated') and explains what each would look like in a text
Points to features of an exemplar that justify its band on a given criterion
Ranks two or three exemplars on one criterion and justifies the ranking with textual evidence
Notes which criteria carry most weight and allocates effort accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two adjacent bands from a rubric criterion (for example, use of sources) and two short exemplar paragraphs. Ask which band each paragraph fits and why. Look for justifications that cite specific textual features linked to the criterion wording rather than general impressions such as 'it sounds more academic'.

topics.name: Grading systems
topics.description: Understand how marks are expressed and interpreted in the learner's institution (for example, UK percentage bands and undergraduate degree classifications, master's pass, merit and distinction thresholds, or GPA-style systems) and what grade bands signal about the quality of work, so that marks are neither over- nor under-interpreted against expectations carried over from other systems.
masteryEvidence: Converts a mark into its band or classification under the local scheme and explains what the band indicates about quality
Explains why, in many UK disciplines, marks above about 80% are uncommon and a mark in the 60s can represent good work, contrasting this with systems they know
Identifies the pass mark and the progression or classification rules for their programme
Interprets a mark alongside the written feedback and criteria rather than on its own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Tell the learner they have received 62% for an undergraduate essay at a UK university and ask what this means, how it compares with their previous system, and what information they would need to improve it. Look for correct interpretation (typically the upper second-class band) and recognition that the criteria and feedback, not the number alone, show how to improve.

topics.name: Feedback literacy
topics.description: Understand feedback as information that learners must actively make sense of and use, not something simply delivered to them. This involves appreciating its purpose, developing the capacity to make evaluative judgements, managing emotional responses and taking action (Carless and Boud's four features). Feedback is recognised in many forms: written comments, rubric marks, peer comments, discussion in class, tutorials and automated tools.
masteryEvidence: Identifies several sources of feedback in a module, including informal and peer feedback, beyond comments on marked work
Explains what a given comment asks them to do differently
Describes their own emotional response to critical feedback and a strategy for engaging with it constructively
Distinguishes comments directed at the task, the process, self-regulation and the person, and explains which are most useful for future work
Gives an example of feedback they acted on and what resulted
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present five feedback comments of different types (praise of the person, a task-level correction, process advice, a question prompting self-monitoring, a vague comment). Ask the learner to rank them by usefulness and explain. Look for recognition that process-level and self-regulation-level comments carry over to future work, and that praise of the person gives little direction.

topics.name: Acting on feedback
topics.description: Turn feedback into a feed-forward action plan: categorise comments, identify issues that recur across assignments, decide which apply to the next (often different) task, act on them and check whether the change worked.
masteryEvidence: Groups comments from several pieces of work into recurring themes
Distinguishes task-specific comments from those that apply to future assignments
Writes an action plan with specific, checkable actions for each priority comment
Shows in a later draft or task where and how each action was implemented
Uses a short feedback-response note ('In this draft I have tried to…') to direct the marker's attention
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner feedback from two previous assignments and the brief for a new, different task. Ask which comments apply and what they will do differently. Look for transfer of process-level comments (for example, on paragraph focus or source integration) and specific actions, rather than a restatement of the comments.

topics.name: Using written corrective feedback
topics.description: Use written corrective feedback on language (direct corrections, correction codes, underlining or margin indications) to understand the nature of errors, self-correct where feedback is indirect, and track recurring error patterns, recognising that one-off corrections rarely carry over to new writing without follow-up.
masteryEvidence: Interprets a course's correction code and states the rule or pattern behind each coded error
Self-corrects indirectly marked errors and explains the corrections
Distinguishes rule-governed errors (for example subject–verb agreement, articles with countable nouns) from less rule-governed ones (word choice, collocation) and uses different resources for each
Keeps an error log that tallies recurring categories across texts
Edits a new text by checking specifically for their most frequent error categories
topics.assessmentPrompt: Return a paragraph in which five errors are indicated by code but not corrected. Ask the learner to correct each and explain why. Check the accuracy of the corrections and the explanations, and ask whether any of these errors also recur in their other writing.

topics.name: Seeking feedback
topics.description: Request feedback that is specific, timely and usable (on a draft, plan or idea) from tutors, supervisors and peers, framing the request politely and within institutional norms, such as what tutors may comment on before submission, and following up to clarify comments.
masteryEvidence: Writes a feedback request that names the specific aspect to be commented on and why
Checks module or programme rules on pre-submission feedback before asking
Uses suitable mitigation and timing in requests to staff, for example giving sufficient notice and acknowledging workload
Asks follow-up questions that clarify a comment's meaning or request an example of what improvement would look like
Seeks feedback from peers and support services as well as from the assessor
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a short email to a module tutor requesting feedback on an essay plan. Check that it names specific questions, shows the work done, respects norms and timing, and is appropriately mitigated. 'Please check my essay' with an attachment sent the day before the deadline indicates a gap.

topics.name: Self- and peer-assessment
topics.description: Judge the quality of one's own and peers' work against criteria and exemplars, give feedback that is specific and criterion-referenced, and calibrate these judgements over time by comparing them with tutors' judgements. The aim is evaluative judgement, not self-grading.
masteryEvidence: Rates a draft against criteria and cites textual evidence for each rating
Gives peer comments that identify a specific issue, explain its effect on the reader and suggest a direction, rather than offering generic praise or proofreading
Compares their own judgements with tutor judgements and identifies where and why they diverge
Uses insights from reviewing others' texts to revise their own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to self-assess a recent draft against two criteria before seeing the tutor's assessment, then compare the two. Look for ratings backed by evidence and, after comparison, an explanation of any divergence (for example, 'I counted my citations; the tutor was looking at how I evaluated them'). Large gaps that the learner cannot explain indicate weak calibration.

topics.name: University exam formats
topics.description: Understand the main formats of university examination (unseen and seen written papers, open-book and take-home exams, multiple-choice and short-answer tests, problem-based papers, oral and practical examinations such as OSCEs in health programmes, and computer-based or online variants) and what kind of knowledge and performance each rewards, so that preparation and in-exam behaviour match the format.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the format of each exam on their programme using handbooks and past papers
Explains how preparation differs for seen, unseen, open-book and objective-format exams
Identifies what each format typically rewards (recall, application, synthesis or performance)
Locates and uses past papers, exam regulations and information on permitted materials
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three brief exam descriptions (a seen-question paper, a 24-hour open-book paper, a multiple-choice test across the whole syllabus) and ask how preparation should differ for each. Look for format-specific preparation (planning answers to seen questions, organising and indexing materials for open-book, retrieval practice across the syllabus for multiple choice) rather than 'revise everything'.

topics.name: Analysing exam questions
topics.description: Analyse an exam question quickly and accurately, identifying the command word or words, topic, focus and limiting words, implicit sub-questions and the expected answer type, and allocate time across questions in proportion to marks.
masteryEvidence: Marks the command, topic, focus and limiting words in a question and paraphrases what it requires
Identifies multi-part questions and implicit sub-questions, such as the judgement of degree required by 'to what extent'
Distinguishes questions inviting description from those requiring evaluation or argument
Allocates time per question in proportion to marks, including time for planning and checking
Recognises when a question that superficially matches a revised topic actually asks for something different
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three exam questions on the same topic with different command words and limiting phrases (for example, 'Outline…', 'Critically evaluate… with reference to…', 'To what extent… since 2010?'). Ask the learner what a good answer to each would do. Look for distinctions in the shape of the answer and attention to limiting words; treating all three as 'write about the topic' indicates a gap.

topics.name: Planning revision
topics.description: Plan revision as a spaced, active schedule that begins weeks before the exam period: mapping the syllabus and past-paper demands, distributing sessions across topics, building sessions around retrieval and timed practice, and adjusting the plan according to self-test results.
masteryEvidence: Produces a revision timetable that starts several weeks before exams and revisits each topic more than once
Builds sessions around retrieval (self-testing, past questions, blank-page recall) rather than rereading
Uses self-test results to move time towards weaker topics
Includes timed practice under exam-like conditions for written papers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show their revision plan for an upcoming exam. Check the start date, spacing and revisiting of topics, the types of activity and the use of past papers; a plan that consists of reading notes once per topic in the final week indicates a gap.

topics.name: Timed writing
topics.description: Produce coherent, relevant written answers under time pressure: planning rapidly (a brief outline and a position), allocating time between planning, writing and checking, writing fluently without sources to hand, and checking for one's own most frequent errors. Applies to exam essays, short-answer papers and timed tasks in language tests and progression assessments.
masteryEvidence: Spends a small, planned share of the available time on a brief outline with a position before writing
Produces an answer whose opening addresses the question directly and whose paragraphs each advance the answer
Completes all required answers within the time, prioritising by marks
Reserves time to check for their own known high-frequency errors
Adapts memorised content to the specific question rather than reproducing it wholesale
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set an unseen question with a fixed time limit and observe the first few minutes. Then examine the script: is there a visible plan, does the introduction answer the question, does each paragraph advance a point, and was the final section completed? Compare the plan with the script to see whether planning was used or abandoned.

topics.name: Objective question strategies
topics.description: Approach multiple-choice, true/false, matching and short-item questions strategically: reading stems precisely (including negatives and qualifiers), predicting an answer before reading the options, eliminating distractors for stated reasons, managing time and flagged items, and applying the paper's rules on guessing and negative marking.
masteryEvidence: Identifies negatives, absolutes and qualifiers in a stem or option and explains how they change the answer
Generates an answer from knowledge before viewing the options when the stem allows
Eliminates options for specific reasons and returns to flagged items
Applies the stated scoring rules, such as negative marking, when deciding whether to answer uncertain items
Distinguishes items testing recall from those testing application and adjusts reading time accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five multiple-choice items from the learner's subject (or based on a general academic text), including one 'NOT' item, one with an absolute qualifier and one application item. Ask the learner to think aloud while answering. Look for close reading of qualifiers, reasoned elimination and correct handling of the negative; choosing options because their wording looks familiar indicates surface processing.

topics.name: Open-book and take-home exams
topics.description: Prepare for and complete open-book and take-home exams, recognising that they assess application, analysis and synthesis rather than recall: organising and indexing permitted materials in advance, managing extended time windows, and observing paper-specific rules on collaboration, sources, citation and AI use.
masteryEvidence: Prepares an organised, indexed set of notes and sources that can be navigated quickly
Answers by applying and synthesising material rather than reproducing notes or lecture slides
Cites sources in take-home answers to the standard the paper requires
States the rules on collaboration, permitted resources and AI use for a given paper and plans to work within them
Plans time across a take-home window, including breaks and a final check
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a take-home question and the learner's own notes on the topic. Ask them to sketch an answer plan in a short, fixed time and to state what they may and may not do (consult peers, use AI tools, reuse lecture slides). Look for application rather than reproduction of notes, an accurate statement of the rules and planned citation.

topics.name: Oral examinations
topics.description: Prepare for and perform in oral assessments such as questioning on submitted work, individual oral examinations, interactive orals and the speaking components of language assessments: anticipating question types, structuring spoken answers, asking for clarification or repetition, gaining thinking time appropriately and recovering from breakdowns.
masteryEvidence: Anticipates likely questions from the assessment's purpose and prepares flexible answer outlines rather than memorised scripts
Gives a direct answer first, then a justification and an example, at an appropriate length
Asks for clarification or repetition of a question rather than guessing its meaning
Uses holding phrases to gain thinking time without long silences
Recovers from a word-finding gap or an error by reformulating rather than abandoning the answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run a short mock oral on a piece of the learner's own work, including one deliberately ambiguous question and one challenging follow-up. Look for a direct-answer structure, a clarification request in response to the ambiguous question, and reformulation rather than breakdown under the follow-up.

topics.name: Managing test anxiety
topics.description: Recognise how anxiety in evaluative situations (written exams, timed tests, oral assessments and high-stakes proficiency tests) can interfere with performance, particularly through worry that takes up attention, and use preparation, reappraisal and in-exam techniques to reduce its impact, while knowing when anxiety calls for professional support or reasonable adjustments.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the worry (cognitive) and physical or emotional components of their own exam anxiety

Uses at least one technique before the exam (for example, brief writing about worries, or reinterpreting arousal as readiness) and one during it (for example, starting with a question they are confident about, or a planned breathing pause)
Explains how realistic timed practice reduces uncertainty about the exam
Identifies the institutional route to support and adjustments when anxiety is severe
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to describe what happens to them in the first ten minutes of a high-stakes exam and what they currently do about it. Look for a distinction between thoughts and physical symptoms and at least one specific, plausible technique. Do not attempt to diagnose; the aim is to see whether the learner has a usable repertoire and knows where to get help.

topics.name: Proficiency, achievement and progression assessment
topics.description: Distinguish the purposes of different language assessments (proficiency, placement, diagnostic, achievement, and progression or gatekeeping decisions) and understand that a score is evidence supporting a particular interpretation and decision, not a fixed property of the learner. This helps learners interpret their results realistically and use each assessment for its intended purpose.
masteryEvidence: Classifies assessments they have taken or will take by purpose (an entry test, a placement test, a weekly quiz, a post-entry diagnostic task, a progression assessment)
Explains what decision each assessment informs and who uses the result
Explains why a proficiency test score cannot show what was learned on a particular course, and why a course test cannot certify general proficiency
Recognises that small score differences may fall within measurement error and may not reflect a real difference in ability
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present four assessments (a university's post-entry diagnostic writing task, an international proficiency test, an end-of-unit grammar quiz and a pre-sessional final project). Ask what each is for, who uses the result and for what decision. Look for reasoning about purpose and decision, and for recognition that a diagnostic result is used to guide support, not to decide admission.

topics.name: CEFR levels and entry requirements
topics.description: Understand what CEFR levels describe (communicative ability in can-do terms across activities, including 'plus' levels and uneven profiles across skills), how university and visa entry requirements are expressed through test scores and levels, and why the relationship between a test score and a CEFR level rests on test owners' published alignment claims, which are approximate and debated. Requirements are set by institutions and government bodies and change over time.
masteryEvidence: Explains what a CEFR level describes and why a learner's profile can differ across skills
Reads a programme's entry requirement (overall and minimum component scores) and determines whether a given score profile meets it
