Explains that alignments between tests and the CEFR are published by test owners, are approximate, and do not make scores from different tests interchangeable
Distinguishes institutional entry requirements from immigration requirements, using the UK Student route as an example, and identifies the official source for checking current rules
Explains why meeting the entry threshold does not guarantee readiness for all the language demands of a programme
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a programme's entry requirement (an overall score plus minimum component scores) and three score profiles from the same test, one of which meets the overall requirement but misses a component minimum. Ask which profiles meet the requirement and why, and where the learner would check whether it also satisfies current visa rules. Look for attention to component minimums and to current official sources rather than agents or forums.

topics.name: Academic proficiency test formats
topics.description: Understand the task types and constructs of the major academic English proficiency tests used for university entry (for example, reading with selected-response items, lecture-style listening, independent and integrated writing, and interview-based or computer-delivered speaking), including differences in delivery mode and in human, automated or hybrid scoring, so that preparation targets what each test actually measures.
masteryEvidence: Describes the task types in the test they will take and the skills or constructs each targets
Identifies differences in delivery (paper, computer, remote) and scoring (human, automated) that affect preparation
Locates the test's official public assessment criteria for productive tasks and explains each criterion in their own words
Uses official sample materials to work out what tasks require rather than relying on unofficial 'tricks'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to describe the writing and speaking tasks of the test they intend to take and the criteria used to score them. Look for accurate task descriptions, criterion names explained in their own words, and awareness of delivery and scoring mode; inaccurate or trick-based descriptions indicate reliance on unofficial sources.

topics.name: Test tasks versus university tasks
topics.description: Recognise how proficiency-test tasks differ from university tasks. Test writing is typically short, timed, drawn from personal knowledge or brief inputs, on general topics and scored against generic criteria; university writing is typically extended, source-based, discipline-specific, varied in genre and judged against disciplinary expectations. Learners use this understanding to avoid carrying test templates into university work.
masteryEvidence: Compares a test writing task with a university assignment brief in terms of length, sources, audience, genre, time and criteria
Identifies test-preparation habits (memorised openings, opinion without sources, formulaic linking) that would weaken a university text
Explains why a high test score does not demonstrate control of source-based disciplinary writing
Rewrites a test-style paragraph as a source-based academic paragraph for a specified discipline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Place a test-style opinion essay prompt next to a first-year assignment brief on a similar topic. Ask the learner to list five differences in what each requires and to say which of their test-preparation habits they would need to drop. Look for the difference in source use, differences of genre and audience, and named habits rather than 'university is harder'.

topics.name: Integrated test tasks
topics.description: Handle integrated test tasks that require reading and/or listening before writing or speaking: noting key points from the input efficiently, identifying the relationship between sources (for example, a talk that challenges a reading), selecting and transforming content in one's own words, and organising the response around the task's specific demand within the time limit.
masteryEvidence: Takes notes on the input that capture the main points and the relationships between sources
Selects the source content the task requires rather than summarising everything
Reports source content in their own words with clear attribution to the reading or speaker
Organises the response around the relationship the task specifies, such as how a talk challenges a reading
Completes the response within the time, dividing it between processing the input and producing the response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Use a short reading and a brief talk that challenges it, then ask for a short written response explaining how the talk relates to the reading. Look for the key points from both, an explicit relationship, attribution and transformed wording; copying strings from the reading or omitting the talk indicates a gap.

topics.name: Pre-sessional progression assessment
topics.description: Understand how pre-sessional and similar pathway programmes assess progression, typically through coursework such as an extended source-based essay or report, a small research project, presentations or seminars, portfolios and sometimes timed tasks, and how criteria, weightings, integrity rules and progression thresholds work, so that learners can plan effort across components and use formative stages.
masteryEvidence: Describes each assessed component of their programme, its weighting and the criteria applied
Explains how component results combine into a progression decision, including any minimum per skill
Uses formative stages (outline, draft, tutorial) to improve the summative submission
Explains integrity expectations specific to coursework-based progression, such as rules on drafts, sources, AI tools and proofreading
Contrasts progression assessment with the proficiency test they might otherwise have taken
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to explain, using their programme handbook, how their progression decision will be made and what they would do if draft feedback identified a weakness in source use. Look for an accurate account of components, weightings and thresholds, and a plan that uses formative feedback and support rather than waiting for the final mark.

topics.name: How universities are organised
topics.description: Identify the organisational units (faculty, school, department, programme, module), staff roles (module leader, personal tutor, programme director, supervisor, professional services staff) and decision-making processes (programme regulations, assessment boards, student representation) that affect one's study, and use this knowledge to find information and the right person to contact. Organisational knowledge underpins effective help-seeking and correspondence, and terms and structures vary considerably between institutions and countries.
masteryEvidence: Locates, in a real programme or module handbook, who is responsible for teaching, assessment, extensions and pastoral support

Distinguishes academic roles (module leader, personal tutor, supervisor) from professional services roles (programme administrator, student support adviser) and states which to contact for a given issue
Explains how modules, credits and programme regulations combine to determine progression and the final award at their own institution
Identifies where formal decisions are made (for example, assessment or extenuating circumstances boards) and what students can and cannot influence
Notes differences between the current institution and previous educational experience without treating either as the norm
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner their programme handbook and three scenarios (illness in the week of a deadline, a question about a lecture concept, a timetable clash). Ask whom they would contact first and where they found that. Check that each issue is routed to the correct role or process, that a handbook location is given, and that the learner does not default to the most senior academic for every problem.

topics.name: Teaching and learning formats
topics.description: Recognise the purposes, participation expectations and preparation demands of the main formats of university teaching (lectures, seminars, tutorials, laboratory and studio sessions, workshops, and VLE-based or blended learning) and the relationship between timetabled contact and independent study. Knowing what each format is for lets learners prepare appropriately and interpret what counts as taking part.
masteryEvidence: States, for each format on their timetable, its main purpose and what students are expected to do before, during and after it
Distinguishes formats in which listening and note-making dominate from those in which spoken contribution, practical work or critique is expected
Estimates the expected independent study time for a module from its credit value and contact hours and plans the week accordingly
Identifies the VLE resources attached to a module (recordings, readings, discussion boards, quizzes) and the role each plays in the module's design
Recognises that the same label (for example 'tutorial' or 'seminar') can denote different formats across departments and institutions, and checks local usage
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner one week's timetable and the VLE page for a real module. Ask what they would do to prepare for each session and what participation each session expects. Check that preparation for a lecture is distinguished from preparation for a seminar or lab, that independent study is planned, and that not every session is treated as content delivery.

topics.name: Expectations of university learners
topics.description: Interpret commonly stated expectations of university learners (independent study, critical engagement with sources, contribution to discussion, responsibility for one's own learning) as situated practices whose meaning varies by discipline, level and institution, rather than as fixed personal traits. Making these expectations concrete helps learners act on them and recognise where their prior experience already meets them.
masteryEvidence: Translates abstract expectations in programme documents (for example 'independent' or 'critical') into concrete behaviours for a specific module
Compares the expectations of two modules or levels and identifies where they differ
Identifies which of their existing study practices already meet stated expectations and which need adapting
Plans a week of independent study that reflects the module's stated learning hours and reading demands
Explains why 'critical thinking' and 'participation' are interpreted differently across disciplines and teachers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a module's learning outcomes or a programme's graduate attributes. Ask them to list three things a student would actually do in this module to meet one outcome. Check for concrete, observable behaviours tied to the module (not general virtues such as 'work hard') and for awareness that interpretations may vary.

topics.name: Discourse communities and disciplines
topics.description: Understand disciplines and other academic groups as discourse communities with shared goals, channels of communication, characteristic genres and specialised lexis, in which membership develops through participation over time. The concept helps learners see academic conventions as purposeful practices of particular communities rather than universal rules, while recognising that communities are internally diverse and their boundaries contested.
masteryEvidence: Describes their target discipline in terms of its goals, communication channels, valued genres and specialised vocabulary
Identifies at least two genres valued in their field and explains what each does for the community
Explains how newcomers gain membership (for example through assessed genres, supervision, conferences) and where they currently stand
Distinguishes conventions shared across academic communities from those specific to their discipline
Recognises disagreement and variation within a community rather than presenting it as homogeneous
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to profile their discipline as a discourse community using five prompts (goals, genres, lexis, channels, who judges quality). Check whether examples are discipline-specific rather than generically academic, and whether internal variation is acknowledged.

topics.name: Disciplinary knowledge-making
topics.description: Compare how disciplines construct knowledge (what counts as evidence, how claims are warranted, the role of theory, cumulative versus interpretive knowledge-building) and relate these differences to the genres, citation practices and stance valued in one's own field. Recognising epistemological difference explains why writing advice that works in one field misleads in another.
masteryEvidence: Describes what counts as legitimate evidence in their own field and contrasts it with a field of a different type (for example hard-pure versus soft-applied)
Relates a feature of disciplinary epistemology to a concrete textual feature such as citation density, hedging or self-mention
Identifies a threshold concept or characteristic way of thinking in their field and explains why it is troublesome for newcomers
Evaluates the usefulness and limits of broad typologies such as hard/soft and pure/applied for describing their own, possibly interdisciplinary, field
Adapts a piece of general writing advice to fit the knowledge-making practices of their discipline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two short extracts on a similar topic from contrasting disciplines (for example epidemiology and sociology). Ask what kind of evidence each relies on and how each signals confidence. Check that differences are linked to how each field builds and warrants knowledge, not merely to topic or individual style.

topics.name: Tacit expectations
topics.description: Identify the unstated conventions behind university tasks and feedback, such as what tutors mean by 'argument', 'structure', 'critical' or 'too descriptive', how criteria are applied in practice, and which behaviours are valued but not taught, and use questioning, exemplars and feedback to make them explicit. Tacit expectations disadvantage students whose prior schooling did not share them, so surfacing them is a matter of equity as well as skill.
masteryEvidence: Identifies evaluative terms in feedback or criteria whose meaning is not self-evident and formulates questions to clarify them
Infers tacit expectations by comparing higher- and lower-graded exemplars and states them as explicit principles
Distinguishes expectations stated in documents from those that are only implied in feedback or practice
Recognises that different tutors may hold different tacit expectations for the same term, and checks rather than generalises
Uses office hours, feedback requests or peers deliberately to test hypotheses about what is expected
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three authentic feedback comments ('needs more argument', 'too descriptive', 'good structure but lacks criticality'). Ask what each means and what they would change. Check whether each comment is translated into a specific textual action, ambiguity is flagged, and a clarifying question is proposed, rather than the comment being guessed at or treated as a language error.

topics.name: Academic literacies perspective
topics.description: Understand the academic literacies view of reading and writing as social practices shaped by identity, power and institutional context, as distinct from study-skills and academic socialisation models, and use it to interpret one's own experience of feedback, conventions and voice. The perspective reframes difficulty as arising from contested and often unstated expectations rather than from individual deficit.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the study skills, academic socialisation and academic literacies models and shows how each would explain the same writing difficulty
Analyses a feedback exchange in terms of differing tutor and student interpretations of what the task required
Identifies a point in their own writing where institutional conventions and their preferred identity or voice were in tension, and explains how they negotiated it
Explains why the perspective treats conventions as negotiable while acknowledging the real consequences of not meeting them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a short case: a student is repeatedly told both to 'use your own voice' and to 'support every claim with sources'. Ask the learner to explain the student's difficulty first from a study-skills and then from an academic literacies perspective. Check whether the second explanation addresses contested expectations, identity and institutional responsibility, not only skill gaps.

topics.name: Transition and adjustment
topics.description: Manage academic and sociocultural adjustment to a new educational context by identifying specific unfamiliar practices and sources of stress, learning the practices of the new setting, drawing on prior knowledge and multilingual repertoires, and building peer, academic and professional support. Adjustment is uneven and individual rather than a fixed sequence of stages, and it involves the institution adapting as well as the student.
masteryEvidence: Identifies specific academic and social demands of the new context that differ from prior experience and plans a response to each
Names at least three sources of support (academic, peer, professional services) and has used at least one
Describes their adjustment in terms of concrete practices learned rather than a generalised 'culture shock' narrative
Identifies prior educational experience and languages as resources they have drawn on, not only as obstacles
Monitors wellbeing and academic progress over a term and adjusts strategies in response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to talk or write for five minutes about one academic practice that surprised them on arrival and what they did about it. Check for a specific practice, a concrete action taken (asking, observing, using a service) and reflection on what transferred from prior experience, rather than general statements about cultural difference.

topics.name: Academic roles and forms of address
topics.description: Choose appropriate forms of address and reference for academic and professional staff (titles such as Dr and Professor, first names, or no title) by checking local practice, the person's own signature or introduction, and the institutional relationship. Norms vary across institutions, countries, disciplines and individuals, and misjudged address in either direction can affect how a message is received.
masteryEvidence: Uses the recipient's email signature, staff profile or self-introduction as evidence when choosing a form of address
Defaults to title plus family name when local norms are unclear, and adjusts when invited to use a first name
Distinguishes academic titles (Dr, Professor) and explains why they are not interchangeable in many systems
Avoids address forms likely to sound marked in the local context, such as a bare role noun used as a title
Refers appropriately to third parties in correspondence (for example 'my supervisor, Dr Rahman')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner four short staff signatures or profiles (a professor, a lecturer with a doctorate who signs with a first name, a programme administrator, a graduate teaching assistant). Ask how they would open an email to each. Check that choices are justified from the evidence given, that a safe default is used where evidence is lacking, and that the learner can explain when first-name address is acceptable.

topics.name: Critical perspectives on EAP
topics.description: Examine whose norms EAP teaches, whose interests they serve and how they might be questioned or negotiated, including native-speaker standards, the dominance of English in scholarship and the pragmatic aim of fitting students to existing demands, and identify where learners can exercise informed choice or seek change. A critical perspective supports agency without pretending that conventions carry no consequences.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes a pragmatic (accommodating) from a critical rationale for teaching a given convention
Identifies a requirement in their own context whose justification is contested and sets out reasoned arguments on more than one side
Explains how the dominance of English in publishing and higher education creates advantages and costs for differently positioned scholars
Proposes a legitimate means of questioning or negotiating a requirement (for example a query to a tutor or use of student representation) and anticipates its consequences
Treats their multilingual and prior academic resources as legitimate contributions to knowledge-making
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short policy statement (for example 'All written work must be in standard British English'). Ask who benefits from the requirement, what it might exclude, and what a student could legitimately do about it. Check for reasoned analysis of interests and consequences rather than either uncritical acceptance or blanket dismissal.

topics.name: EMI and transnational education contexts
topics.description: Understand the conditions of studying through English in non-anglophone universities (English-medium instruction) and in transnational provision such as branch campuses and franchised or joint programmes, including the roles of English and other languages, content lecturers' varied expectations about language, and what this implies for the academic English that matters locally. EMI and TNE learners need academic English shaped by their actual context rather than by anglophone-campus assumptions.
masteryEvidence: Describes the language ecology of their programme: which languages are used for which purposes and by whom
Identifies whether and how content lecturers attend to language, and where language support is or is not provided
Distinguishes intelligibility and disciplinary precision from conformity to a particular national variety as goals for their own English
Draws strategically on other languages for comprehension and discussion where the programme permits
Explains how regulations and assessment in transnational programmes may follow the awarding institution's norms rather than local ones
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to map a typical week on their own (or a described) EMI programme: which language is used for lectures, readings, discussion, assessment and informal talk, and by whom. Check that actual practice is distinguished from official policy and that the learner draws a conclusion about which English skills matter most in that context.

topics.name: Politeness and face in academic interaction
topics.description: Analyse student–staff and peer interaction in terms of face, social distance, relative power and the size of an imposition, and choose linguistic strategies (mitigation, indirectness, acknowledging the other's time and autonomy) accordingly. Politeness norms depend on context and vary across institutions and individuals, so the aim is informed choice rather than a single formula.
masteryEvidence: Estimates the relative power, social distance and imposition in a given academic interaction and justifies the estimate
Identifies mitigation devices (modal verbs, conditional and past-tense forms, hedges, reasons, acknowledgements of imposition) in authentic messages
Adjusts the degree of mitigation of the same act for different recipients and levels of imposition
Recognises excessive deference and over-elaboration as potential problems, not only under-mitigation
Explains why a message acceptable in one setting may be read as abrupt or as overly formal in another
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two versions of the same request to a lecturer, one unmitigated and one heavily over-mitigated. Ask how each might be perceived and to write a version in between. Check that the learner names power, distance and imposition, keeps the request clear, and avoids both bare imperatives and extended deference.

topics.name: Emails to academic staff
topics.description: Write emails to lecturers, supervisors and professional services staff with an informative subject line, an appropriate greeting and form of address, an early statement of purpose, sufficient context, a clear request or question, and a suitable closing and signature with identifying details. Email is often the first and most frequent written contact with staff, and its form shapes perceptions of the writer.
masteryEvidence: Writes subject lines that identify the module or topic and the purpose of the message
Opens with an appropriate greeting and form of address and closes with a conventional sign-off, full name and, where relevant, student number and programme
States the purpose in the first or second sentence and keeps to one main purpose per email
Provides enough context for the recipient to act without further queries, and no more
Checks register, accuracy and tone before sending, and uses the institutional account
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a scenario (they cannot access a required reading and the seminar is in two days) and ten minutes to write the email. Check the subject line, address form, early purpose statement, sufficient context, proportionately mitigated request, closing with identifying details, and the absence of over-familiar phrasing or unexplained demands for an immediate reply.

topics.name: Making requests
topics.description: Make academic requests (for extensions, meetings, references, clarification, feedback or resources) in writing and speech that state clearly what is wanted, give a relevant reason, and are mitigated in proportion to the imposition. Clarity of purpose and appropriate mitigation together determine whether a request is understood and granted, and some requests must go through formal procedures rather than personal appeal.
masteryEvidence: States the request explicitly and early, specifying an action and timeframe the recipient can respond to
Supports the request with a relevant reason and any information or evidence the recipient needs
Uses internal modification (could/would, conditional clauses, 'possible') and external modification proportionate to the imposition
Avoids imposing obligations or deadlines on the recipient unless genuine urgency is explained
Checks institutional procedures first and frames procedurally governed requests, such as extensions, accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write two requests: a low-imposition one (a link to a missing reading) and a high-imposition one (a reference letter needed in five days). Check that directness and mitigation differ appropriately between them, that the request is unambiguous, that a reason is given, and that any relevant procedure or timescale is acknowledged.

topics.name: Office hours and tutorials
topics.description: Prepare for and conduct one-to-one or small-group meetings with academic staff: booking through the expected channel, bringing specific questions and materials, framing the purpose at the start, negotiating and checking understanding, noting agreed actions and closing within the time available. These meetings are a key but under-used route to tacit expectations and individual feedback.
masteryEvidence: Books or attends the meeting through the expected channel and states its purpose in advance where required
Prepares two or three specific questions with relevant materials (a draft, feedback, notes)
Opens by framing the purpose and closes by summarising agreed actions
Asks follow-up and clarification questions and confirms understanding of advice before the meeting ends
Manages time and recognises the staff member's closing signals
topics.assessmentPrompt: Role-play a ten-minute office hour in which the 'tutor' gives brief and somewhat vague advice on a draft. Check whether the learner states a clear purpose, asks specific questions, seeks clarification of the vague advice, summarises next steps and closes appropriately.

topics.name: Formal statements and appeals
topics.description: Write formal institutional texts (extenuating or mitigating circumstances statements, academic appeals and complaints) that follow the relevant procedure, give a factual, chronological and evidenced account, relate it to the grounds the regulations allow, state the outcome sought and keep a measured, non-accusatory tone. These texts affect progression and are judged against regulations, so procedural fit matters more than persuasion or emotional appeal.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the correct procedure, deadline and evidence requirements from institutional regulations before writing
Gives a concise, chronological factual account with dates, linking each circumstance to its effect on assessment
States the specific outcome requested and relates it to grounds the regulations permit
Maintains a measured register, avoiding accusation, emotional overstatement and appeals to sympathy unsupported by evidence
Distinguishes grounds a procedure accepts from those it excludes (in many institutions, disagreement with academic judgement is not itself a ground for appeal)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an extract from an extenuating circumstances policy and a disordered narrative of events. Ask for a 150-word statement. Check that relevant facts are selected and ordered chronologically with dates, that circumstances are linked to their effect on assessment, that a permitted outcome is requested, and that the tone is measured.

topics.name: Apologising and explaining
topics.description: Apologise and give accounts for missed deadlines, absences, lateness or other lapses in a way that acknowledges responsibility proportionately, explains briefly and relevantly, proposes repair, and avoids both under-apology and excessive self-abasement or over-disclosure. Effective apologies maintain working relationships and often connect the student to the formal process they actually need.
masteryEvidence: Includes an explicit apology expression proportionate to the lapse
Gives a brief, relevant explanation without unnecessary personal detail
Offers or requests a concrete repair (catching up, rescheduling, using the formal absence or extension process)
Distinguishes situations needing a personal apology from those needing a formal procedure, and does both where required
Avoids accounts that shift blame onto the recipient or institution, and avoids repeated self-criticism
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to respond in writing, or orally in role-play, to a seminar tutor after missing two sessions. Check for an explicit apology, a brief relevant account, a repair or plan, reference to any formal absence process, and a proportionate register.

topics.name: Online discussion forum posts
topics.description: Write asynchronous discussion posts and replies on VLE forums that respond to the prompt, make a clear point supported by course readings or evidence, engage explicitly with others' contributions, and use a register between conversation and formal academic prose. Forum posts are often assessed and make reasoning visible to peers, so they reward both argument and collegial engagement.
masteryEvidence: Addresses the prompt directly with a clear point in the opening sentences
Supports the point with reference to course readings or evidence, cited in the form the module expects
Replies to peers by naming and building on, qualifying or respectfully challenging specific points
Uses a register suited to the forum (first person and direct address usually acceptable; no text-speak) and keeps to any length guidance
Moves the discussion forward with a question, new angle or synthesis rather than only agreeing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a forum prompt and two peer posts and ask for a reply of about 150 words. Check that the reply engages a specific peer point, adds supported content, handles agreement or disagreement collegially and uses an appropriate register.

topics.name: Messaging channels and norms
topics.description: Choose the appropriate channel (email, VLE messages or forums, enquiry and ticketing systems, group chats, collaboration platforms) for a given purpose, recipient, level of privacy and urgency, and adjust tone, length and expectations of response time accordingly. Channel norms differ across institutions and teams and are often unstated; a misjudged channel can delay a response or blur professional boundaries.
masteryEvidence: Selects the channel specified by the module or department for each type of query and can show where this is stated
Adjusts register and length when moving between channels (for example a peer group chat versus an email to staff)
Sets realistic expectations about response times and spaces any follow-up messages appropriately
Distinguishes public or shared channels from private ones and judges what information belongs in each
Respects boundaries such as staff working hours and the use of personal accounts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner six scenarios (a general assignment question, a private health matter, arranging a group meeting, an urgent laboratory safety issue, a reference request, a query about a mark). Ask which channel they would use and when they would expect a reply. Check that choices follow stated norms, protect privacy and set realistic expectations.

topics.name: Acknowledgements
topics.description: Write acknowledgements for dissertations, theses and articles that thank supervisors, participants, funders, institutions and others in a conventional order and register, include required funding and contribution statements, and distinguish acknowledgement from authorship. The genre is short but socially significant, combining personal gratitude with institutional and ethical obligations.
masteryEvidence: Organises thanks following conventional moves for the genre (for example a reflecting move, thanking moves and an announcing move accepting responsibility)
Includes required elements such as funding sources and grant numbers in the form the institution or journal specifies
Distinguishes contributors who merit acknowledgement from those who meet authorship criteria
Selects a register more personal than the main text but appropriate for a public academic document
Respects participant confidentiality and any agreed anonymity when thanking participants or organisations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a list of people and bodies (supervisor, anonymous interview participants, a funder with grant number, a statistician who advised on analysis, a partner, a colleague who proofread). Ask for a 120-word thesis acknowledgement and a two-sentence article acknowledgement. Check ordering, inclusion of the funding detail, protection of anonymity, register, and how contributors are handled relative to authorship.

topics.name: Virtual learning environments
topics.description: Navigate the institution’s virtual learning environment and related systems to find module information, assessment briefs, readings, recordings, announcements and feedback; submit work correctly through submission portals; and keep track of deadlines and notifications. Missed instructions, unread feedback and failed submissions are avoidable sources of difficulty, especially in a first term.
masteryEvidence: Locates module handbooks, assessment briefs, marking criteria, reading lists and recordings for a given module
Submits assignments correctly, checking file format, file name and the submission receipt
Retrieves and opens returned feedback, including inline comments and audio or video feedback
Manages notifications and announcements so that key information is not missed
Uses discussion areas and messaging within the platform in line with module expectations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set a 15-minute task on the learner’s actual platform: find the assessment brief, criteria, deadline, submission point and most recent recording for one module, and locate the feedback on a previous submission. Check speed and accuracy, and whether the learner checks the submission receipt and opens the feedback comments rather than looking only at the grade.

topics.name: Reference management software
topics.description: Use reference management software to collect, organise and annotate sources, insert in-text citations and generate reference lists in a required style, and check the output for errors. Reference managers save time and reduce inconsistency, but they reproduce whatever metadata they are given, so users still need to know what a correct reference looks like.
masteryEvidence: Imports references from databases, DOIs and PDFs and corrects incomplete or inaccurate metadata
Organises a library with folders, tags and notes that reflect a project’s themes
Inserts citations and generates a reference list in a specified style through a word-processor plug-in
Checks generated citations and references against the style guide and corrects common errors (capitalisation, missing pages, wrong item type, duplicates)
Backs up and, where relevant, shares a library with collaborators
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sources (a journal article with a DOI, a book chapter, a report, a web page and a dataset) and ask the learner to import them, insert citations into a short paragraph and generate a reference list in the course style. Check metadata accuracy, item types and style compliance, and whether the learner finds and corrects at least two automatic errors.

topics.name: Academic word processing
topics.description: Use the word-processing functions that support academic documents: paragraph and heading styles, automatic numbering, generated contents pages, captions and cross-references, section breaks, headers, footers and page numbers, templates, and comments. Structure-based formatting saves time in long documents, keeps formatting consistent and makes documents accessible and easier to revise.
masteryEvidence: Applies heading styles and generates an automatic table of contents
Inserts captions for tables and figures and cross-references that update automatically
Uses section breaks to manage different page numbering or orientation
Applies a required template or formatting specification (margins, spacing, font) efficiently
Navigates a long document using the navigation pane and styles
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an unformatted ten-page document with manually formatted headings, typed figure numbers and a typed contents list. Ask the learner to restructure it with styles, numbered captions, cross-references and a generated contents page within 30 minutes. Check that headings appear in the navigation pane, the contents page updates, and cross-references update when a figure is moved.

topics.name: Machine translation
topics.description: Use machine translation (MT) strategically and transparently: to support comprehension of difficult texts, to check understanding, to explore wording and, where permitted, to support drafting, while recognising MT’s characteristic errors (terminology, register, lost hedging, ambiguity), verifying its output and complying with assessment rules. MT is a legitimate plurilingual resource, but undeclared or wholesale use in assessed writing can breach integrity policies and bypass language development.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes permitted from prohibited uses of MT in a given assessment according to institutional and module policy
Uses MT to support comprehension while checking key terms against discipline glossaries or dictionaries
Identifies typical MT errors in academic text (mistranslated technical terms, lost or added hedging, register shifts, fluent but inaccurate output)
Post-edits MT output critically and explains the changes made
Declares MT use where required and keeps a record of how it was used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an academic paragraph machine-translated into English from a language the learner reads, containing three seeded errors (a mistranslated technical term, a lost hedge and a register shift). Ask the learner to identify and correct the problems and to say whether this use would be permitted under a given module policy. Check error detection, especially of the lost hedge, and accurate interpretation of the policy.

topics.name: Digital collaboration tools
topics.description: Use shared documents, comments, suggestion and track-changes modes, version history and cloud workspaces to co-author and review academic work: setting permissions, giving and responding to comments constructively and concisely, resolving suggestions, and keeping a clear record of contributions. Digital collaboration is now the default medium for group projects and for much supervisor feedback.
masteryEvidence: Sets up a shared document or workspace with appropriate permissions and a clear structure
Uses suggestion or track-changes mode and comments rather than silently overwriting others’ text
Writes comments that are specific, actionable and appropriately mitigated
Accepts, rejects or replies to suggestions and comments, and resolves threads
Uses version history to recover text and to evidence individual contributions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a shared draft with five comments from a supervisor or peer, some of them ambiguous. Ask the learner to respond to each (accept, reject with a reason, or ask for clarification) using comments and suggestions. Check use of the appropriate functions, the clarity and politeness of replies, and that no text is silently overwritten.

topics.name: File and version management
topics.description: Organise, name, version and back up academic files systematically: consistent folder structures and file names, clear distinction between working and submitted versions, local and off-device backups, and secure storage of sensitive material. Good file management prevents lost work and confusion between drafts and, for research students, is the basis of research data management.
masteryEvidence: Uses a consistent folder structure and file-naming convention (e.g., date, module, version)
Distinguishes working drafts from submitted versions and retrieves any earlier version on request
Maintains at least two backups, one of them off-device, and has tested recovery
Stores sensitive or personal data securely in line with institutional policy
Documents research files and data so that another person could understand and locate them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show where the latest and the submitted versions of their last assignment are, and to explain how they would recover the work if their laptop failed. Check naming consistency, version clarity and the existence of an off-device backup; for research students, check whether research data are stored according to policy.

topics.name: Digital etiquette and online presence
topics.description: Communicate appropriately in digital academic spaces (forums, group chats, video calls, social media and professional networks), adapting tone, formality and response expectations to channel and audience, and manage an academic online presence and privacy (profiles, researcher identifiers, what to share publicly). Digital interactions persist and are searchable, so pragmatic misjudgements can have lasting effects.
masteryEvidence: Adapts formality, length and tone to the channel and relationship (course forum, group chat, professional network)
Follows participation norms in video calls (camera, microphone, chat, turn-taking)
Creates and maintains an accurate, professional academic profile appropriate to their stage, such as an institutional profile or researcher identifier
Makes informed decisions about privacy and about what personal or research information to share publicly
Recognises online conflict or inappropriate content and responds through appropriate channels
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three scenarios: a group-chat message to a peer who has missed a deadline; a forum reply disagreeing with a classmate; a public post about one’s own research. Ask the learner to draft each. Check register shifts across channels, mitigation in disagreement, and awareness of public visibility and confidentiality.

topics.name: Automated writing evaluation tools
topics.description: Use automated writing evaluation (AWE) tools, including grammar and style checkers, automated feedback platforms and AI-based feedback features, as one input among others: interpret their suggestions critically, accept or reject them on principled grounds, recognise what they cannot judge (argument, content, disciplinary appropriateness) and comply with rules on permitted use. Uncritical acceptance can introduce errors, flatten voice and, where rewriting features are used, breach assessment rules.
masteryEvidence: Explains which kinds of issue AWE tools detect reliably and which they miss or misjudge
Accepts or rejects suggestions with reasons based on grammatical knowledge or disciplinary convention
Identifies false alarms (e.g., flagged technical terms or necessary passives) and missed problems
Combines AWE feedback with teacher and peer feedback in a revision plan
Checks whether a tool’s features, especially rewriting or paraphrasing functions, are permitted for a given assessment
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run one of the learner’s paragraphs through an AWE tool and ask them to work through ten suggestions, accepting or rejecting each with a reason. Check the accuracy of their decisions, especially rejection of inappropriate suggestions (such as replacing a technical term or removing a necessary passive), and whether they notice problems the tool missed.

topics.name: How generative AI works and fails
topics.description: Explain in non-technical terms how large language models generate text — by predicting likely continuations from patterns learned from very large training datasets, with further tuning to follow instructions — and why this produces fluent but unverified output, fabricated facts and references, biases inherited from training data, and gaps beyond the training data. This understanding underpins every judgement about when AI output can be trusted and how it must be checked.
masteryEvidence: Explains that model output is generated from statistical patterns rather than retrieved from a verified database, and draws the implication for accuracy
Predicts tasks on which output is likely to be unreliable, such as specific references, recent events, specialised or local knowledge, exact quotations and calculations
Identifies one-sided framing or bias in an AI output and relates it to training data
Distinguishes tools that generate from their training alone from tools that retrieve and cite documents, and explains why the latter still need checking
Explains why fluent, confident wording is not evidence of accuracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show an AI-generated paragraph on a topic the learner knows, containing a plausible but false statistic and a non-existent reference. Ask how such errors arise and which parts they would check first. Look for an explanation in terms of prediction from patterns rather than 'the AI lied' or 'its database had a mistake'.

topics.name: Interpreting AI policies
topics.description: Locate and interpret the rules on generative AI that apply to a specific task — institutional policy, programme and module guidance, the assessment brief and, for researchers, publisher and funder policies — including which kinds of use are permitted and what must be declared. Policies differ between and within institutions and change over time, so learners need a routine for checking each task and for asking when the rules are unclear.
masteryEvidence: Locates the AI rules for a given assessment and identifies the level or category of use permitted
Applies the rules to specific uses (grammar correction, translation, brainstorming, summarising readings, drafting) and identifies which are allowed
Recognises AI features embedded in everyday tools such as editors, translators and search engines as potentially covered by the policy
Writes a concise clarification request to a tutor when a use is not covered
Re-checks the rules for each module and assessment rather than assuming one rule applies everywhere
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a brief stating a mid-level permission (for example: AI may be used for planning and language feedback but not to generate assessed text, and all use must be declared) and five proposed uses. Ask the learner to classify each and say what would need declaring. Look for task-specific application and recognition of grey areas needing clarification.

topics.name: Acknowledging and citing AI use
topics.description: Declare and, where required, cite generative AI use in the form the institution, assessment or publisher specifies — typically stating which tools were used, for what purpose and at which stage, and keeping prompts and outputs as records — and distinguish acknowledging assistance from citing AI output as content. Transparent records also allow learners to demonstrate their own process if their work is questioned.
masteryEvidence: Writes a declaration stating tool, version or date, purpose, stage of use, and how outputs were evaluated or changed
Formats an in-text citation and reference for quoted or paraphrased AI output in the required style
Keeps a log of prompts, outputs and their own revisions and can produce it on request
Distinguishes uses that require declaration only, citation, or are not permitted
Applies publication norms that AI tools are not listed as authors and that their use is disclosed (PGR)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a declaration for an essay in which they used an AI tool to suggest counter-arguments to consider and to check grammar in the final draft. Check that it specifies tools, purposes, stages and their own evaluation, and is honest and proportionate rather than vague ('I used AI a bit').

topics.name: Verifying AI output
topics.description: Check AI output before relying on it: verify factual claims against authoritative sources, confirm that every reference exists and says what is attributed to it, check quotations and figures against the originals, and look for omissions and bias. Fabricated and erroneous citations are a documented failure of language models, so verification is a non-negotiable step whenever AI output informs academic work.
masteryEvidence: Checks each AI-supplied reference in a library database, publisher site or DOI resolver and identifies fabricated or altered ones
Traces key factual claims to an authoritative source using lateral reading
Compares an AI summary of a text with the text and identifies omissions, distortions and changes in certainty
Identifies missing perspectives or one-sided framing in AI output on a contested topic
Records what was verified, corrected and discarded
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an AI-generated paragraph with three references (one accurate, one real but misdescribed, one non-existent) and two factual claims, and allow ten minutes with library access. Strong performers find all reference problems through databases and check claims against sources rather than against another AI output.

topics.name: Using AI as a language-learning resource
topics.description: Use generative AI to support language development — explanations of grammar and vocabulary, feedback that identifies rather than silently fixes errors, practice dialogues and exercises, and comparison of alternative phrasings — in ways that keep the learner doing the cognitive work and stay within assessment rules. The aim is durable competence, so learners evaluate AI feedback critically and check whether their unassisted writing and speaking improve.
masteryEvidence: Requests feedback that locates and explains errors rather than a corrected version, then self-corrects
Evaluates AI language suggestions, identifying when a change alters meaning, certainty, register or disciplinary terminology
Uses AI to generate targeted practice on a recurring error and tests progress without the tool
Distinguishes the language support permitted for a task from rewriting that would breach its rules
Keeps a record of recurring error patterns identified through AI and other feedback
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to demonstrate how they would use an AI tool to improve a 100-word paragraph of their own for an assessment that permits language feedback but not rewriting. Check whether the prompts elicit explanation rather than replacement text, and whether the learner accepts, rejects or modifies suggestions with reasons.

topics.name: AI, authorship and voice
topics.description: Consider who is the author of a text produced with AI assistance — whose ideas, reasoning and words it contains, and who is accountable for them — and maintain one's own authorial voice and stance when using AI. AI-polished text can become generic and can misrepresent a writer's actual reasoning and competence, so learners decide where assistance must stop for a task to remain their own work.
masteryEvidence: Explains why accountability for content, including errors, rests with the human author
Identifies changes to stance, hedging and positioning in an AI-edited version of their own paragraph
Revises an AI-edited passage to restore their own stance, claims and disciplinary positioning
Justifies a boundary for their own AI use in a task in terms of what the assessment is designed to show
Explains why AI tools are not credited as authors in scholarly publication
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner their own paragraph and an AI-'improved' version. Ask which they would submit, what changed in meaning, stance and voice, and which better represents their reasoning. Look for attention to claims, hedging and stance, not only to fluency.

topics.name: Limits of AI detection
topics.description: Understand that AI-text detectors estimate the likelihood that text was machine-generated, produce both false positives and false negatives, can be evaded, and have been shown to misclassify writing by non-native English writers as AI-generated at high rates. Detector output therefore does not establish misconduct; learners protect themselves by keeping evidence of their writing process and knowing how integrity processes treat such indicators.
masteryEvidence: Explains in plain terms why detectors that rely on measures of predictability can flag simple or formulaic human writing
Summarises evidence that detectors have misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated
Explains why a detector score alone cannot establish misconduct
Keeps evidence of their own writing process (notes, drafts, version history) for assessed work
Rejects 'humanising' or paraphrasing tools as a response to detectors and explains the integrity and quality risks
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask: 'A friend's essay was flagged as 80% AI-generated, but they wrote it themselves. What does the score mean, and what should they do?' Strong answers explain detector unreliability and bias, refer to the institution's process, and propose gathering drafts and version history rather than rewriting the essay to lower the score.

topics.name: Prompting for learning
topics.description: Write prompts that make AI act as a tutor or sparring partner — explanations at a chosen level, Socratic questions, worked examples followed by practice, counter-arguments, or feedback against criteria — rather than producing finished text, and judge whether the interaction produced learning. Effective prompting includes giving context and constraints, iterating, and stopping to work without the tool.
masteryEvidence: Writes prompts that specify role, level, task and constraints, such as asking to be questioned rather than given the answer
Uses AI to generate self-test questions or counter-arguments and answers them without assistance
Iterates a prompt when the output is too generic, too advanced or off-task
Judges whether an interaction increased their understanding by explaining the idea afterwards without the tool
Keeps prompting within the uses permitted for the task
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write two prompts for preparing a seminar on an assigned reading: one that would help them learn and one that would replace their thinking. Check the contrast (questioning, explanation and self-testing versus summary or answer generation) and whether the learning prompt includes constraints and a follow-up step done without the tool.

topics.name: AI-assisted research tools
topics.description: Evaluate and use AI-based literature discovery, question-answering and summarisation tools, understanding their limits in coverage, ranking, reproducibility and accuracy. These tools can speed up orientation to a field, but they cannot replace documented database searching, reading the sources themselves, or the researcher's own judgement of relevance and quality.
masteryEvidence: Compares results from an AI discovery tool with a structured database search on the same question and identifies differences in coverage
Checks AI-generated summaries of papers against the papers and identifies errors in findings, methods or certainty
Explains why AI tool searches are hard to reproduce and document, and records their use appropriately
Uses AI tools to find leads and then reads and cites the primary sources directly
Applies institutional and publisher rules on AI use in literature reviews
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to use an AI research tool on a narrow question in their field, then check the three most important papers it cites. Ask what the tool got right, what it misrepresented or missed, and how they would document its use. Look for checks against full texts rather than abstracts alone.

topics.name: Privacy, data and intellectual property with AI
topics.description: Judge what may and may not be entered into AI tools — personal and research-participant data, confidential or unpublished material, others' copyrighted work, and one's own unpublished work — taking account of the tool's terms on data retention and training, institutional data-protection rules and research ethics approvals. Learners also recognise that copyright in AI-generated content and in training data remains legally unsettled and varies by jurisdiction.
masteryEvidence: Identifies data in a coursework or research scenario that must not be uploaded to a public AI tool and explains why
Checks a tool's terms and institutional guidance on data retention and training use before uploading material
Explains how ethics approvals and consent forms constrain the use of AI tools with participant data
Explains why uploading copyrighted readings or others' unpublished manuscripts, for example when peer reviewing, may breach licences or confidentiality
Chooses institutionally approved tools or anonymisation where AI processing is permitted
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a scenario: a master's student wants to paste interview transcripts into a public chatbot to identify themes. Ask what must be checked first and what alternatives exist. Look for consent and ethics approval, data protection, the tool's data terms, anonymisation and approved tools.

topics.name: The language of science
topics.description: Recognise how scientific English builds knowledge through technical terms organised into taxonomies, chains of interlocking definitions, nominalisation (grammatical metaphor) and high lexical density, and explain what each does for the scientific reader. Understanding these features as functional, not as obscurity, lets learners unpack dense textbook and research prose and begin to produce it.
masteryEvidence: Unpacks a nominalised scientific sentence into a sequence of congruent clauses (who did what, what caused what) and repacks it
Identifies the taxonomic relations (type-of, part-of) among technical terms in a textbook section and represents them as a diagram
Distinguishes a technical term from an everyday word with the same form (work, force, power, stress, solution) and uses each in the right register
Explains how a nominal group such as a process noun lets a writer treat a previous event as the starting point of the next clause
Judges when a nominalisation in their own writing aids flow and when it hides the agent or the causal relation the reader needs
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a two-sentence extract from a first-year science textbook containing at least two nominalisations and one technical term defined earlier in the chapter. Ask them to rewrite it as it might be explained aloud to a classmate, then name which words are technical. Check that they recover the processes and participants hidden in the nominalisations without changing the causal relation and that they keep the technical term rather than replacing it with a loose synonym.

topics.name: Scientific explanations
topics.description: Write and present explanations of how or why phenomena occur, choosing among sequential explanations (a chain of events in time), causal and factorial explanations (multiple causes), consequential explanations (multiple effects) and theoretical explanations that apply a model or law to a case. Explanation is one of the most frequently assessed genres in undergraduate science and engineering and underlies exam answers, lab-report discussions and textbook learning.
masteryEvidence: Selects an explanation type that fits the question (for example a sequential explanation for a cycle, a factorial explanation for a multi-cause outcome)
Opens with an identifying statement of the phenomenon and then stages the explanation in a logically ordered series of steps or factors
Makes causal links explicit with verbs, conjunctions and nominalised causes rather than relying on 'and then'
Integrates a labelled diagram or equation and refers to it at the relevant step
Applies a named model or law to a specific case and states where the model's assumptions limit the explanation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to explain in about 150 words why a metal spoon in hot water feels hotter than a wooden one, or a comparable phenomenon from their subject. Check whether they identify the phenomenon first, order the causal steps, make each causal link explicit, use the relevant technical terms (for example thermal conductivity) correctly and avoid narrating a single experiment instead of explaining the general mechanism.

topics.name: Protocols and specifications
topics.description: Read and write procedural and specification texts used in laboratories and engineering: experimental protocols and standard operating procedures, method statements, and requirements or design specifications. This involves numbered imperative steps with exact quantities, conditions and tolerances, safety notes placed before the hazardous step, and requirement statements that use modal verbs consistently (often shall or must for mandatory, should for recommended, may for optional) so that each statement can be verified.
masteryEvidence: Writes a protocol whose steps another student can follow without asking questions, with quantities, units, conditions and timings stated
Places cautions and warnings before the step they apply to and separates them visually from the instruction
Distinguishes the imperative mood of a protocol from the past passive of a lab-report method and converts between them
Writes requirement statements that are single, unambiguous and testable, and uses modal verbs consistently with the convention the department or standard specifies
Identifies ambiguity in a specification (vague quantifiers, undefined terms, compound requirements) and rewrites it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three faulty requirement statements, for example one that bundles two requirements, one with a vague quantity ('fast', 'approximately') and one that mixes should and must. Ask them to rewrite each so that a tester could pass or fail it. Check for one requirement per statement, measurable criteria with units, and consistent modal use.

topics.name: Language of experimentation
topics.description: Use the language of experimental design and measurement precisely: testable hypotheses and predictions, independent, dependent and controlled variables, control conditions, random and systematic error, accuracy versus precision, and statements of uncertainty (for example with ± and appropriate significant figures). Many of these words have everyday meanings (error, control, significant, precise) that differ from their technical sense, so misuse signals misunderstanding of method as well as of language.
masteryEvidence: Writes a hypothesis and a corresponding prediction that state the expected relationship between named independent and dependent variables
Identifies the controlled variables and the control condition in a described experiment and explains why each is needed
Distinguishes random from systematic error and accuracy from precision, and proposes an appropriate improvement for each
Reports a measured value with its uncertainty and a number of significant figures consistent with that uncertainty
Uses 'significant' only in its statistical sense in results writing, and chooses other wording for importance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short description of a simple experiment with one flaw (for example a thermometer that reads 2 °C high throughout). Ask them to name the variables, state the hypothesis, identify the type of error and say whether it affects accuracy or precision. Check that they classify the flaw as systematic error affecting accuracy, not precision, and that they use the variable terms correctly.

topics.name: Software and technical documentation
topics.description: Write the main documentation genres of computing for their distinct readers: README files that tell a newcomer what a project does and how to install, run and contribute to it; code comments and docstrings that explain intent and non-obvious decisions rather than restating the code; API reference entries that specify parameters, return values, errors and examples; and design documents that set out context, goals and non-goals, alternatives considered and trade-offs. Documentation is assessed in computing projects and is a core professional literacy.
masteryEvidence: Produces a README that a peer can use to install and run the project, with a one-sentence purpose statement, prerequisites, usage example and licence or contribution note
Writes comments that explain why code does something or warn of a non-obvious constraint, and removes comments that merely paraphrase the code
Documents a function or endpoint with parameter types, return values, error conditions and a minimal working example in a consistent format
Writes a design-document section that compares at least two alternatives against stated criteria and justifies the choice
Adjusts terminology and assumed knowledge for end users, contributors and maintainers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 15-line function with no documentation and two existing comments, one useful and one that restates the code. Ask them to write a docstring and decide which comment to keep. Check that the docstring states purpose, parameters, return value and at least one error case, and that they keep the comment explaining intent and delete the redundant one.

topics.name: Mathematical writing and proofs
topics.description: Write proofs and worked solutions in which notation is embedded in grammatical, punctuated sentences and the logical steps are signalled in words: introducing objects (let, suppose, define), stating quantifiers (for all, there exists), marking inference (hence, it follows that, since), naming the proof strategy (by contradiction, by induction, by the contrapositive) and closing the argument. Markers in mathematics expect the reasoning, not only the answer, to be readable, and students used to answer-only assessment often lose marks for unexplained steps.
masteryEvidence: Introduces every symbol before it is used and states its type or domain
Writes each displayed equation as part of a sentence, with connecting words and punctuation, and avoids starting a sentence with a symbol
Distinguishes necessary from sufficient conditions and 'if' from 'if and only if' in their own statements
Announces the proof strategy at the start and signals where each case or the inductive step begins and ends
Justifies each non-trivial step by citing a definition, earlier result or algebraic rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a correct but answer-only solution to a short proof (for example that the sum of two odd integers is even) written as a column of equations. Ask them to rewrite it as a proof a lecturer would accept. Check that they define the integers with appropriate quantifiers, link each line with words such as 'so' or 'hence', state the conclusion in words and punctuate the displayed lines as part of sentences.

topics.name: Evidence-based practice
topics.description: Understand evidence-based practice as the integration of the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the values and circumstances of the patient, not as following research alone. In academic work this means framing focused clinical questions (for example in PICO form), recognising evidence hierarchies and their limits, and writing assignments in which recommendations for practice are justified by appraised evidence, professional judgement and patient perspective.
masteryEvidence: Explains the components of evidence-based practice and why research evidence alone does not determine a care decision
Turns a clinical scenario into a focused, searchable question that names population, intervention, comparison and outcome
Places study designs in a conventional hierarchy of evidence and explains at least one limitation of hierarchies (for example for questions about patient experience)
Justifies a recommendation in an assignment by linking it to appraised evidence, practice context and patient preference
Distinguishes evidence-based statements from tradition- or authority-based ones in a clinical text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short clinical scenario in which the best-supported intervention conflicts with the patient's stated preference. Ask them to write a paragraph recommending a course of action. Check whether they cite the evidence and its strength, acknowledge the patient's values and professional judgement, and avoid presenting the research finding as automatically decisive.

topics.name: Reflective practice writing in health
topics.description: Write structured reflections on placement or practice experiences using a model the programme specifies (for example Gibbs's reflective cycle or a What? So what? Now what? model), moving from a concise, anonymised account of an event to analysis that draws on literature and professional standards, and ending with a concrete plan for future practice. Reflective writing is assessed throughout health programmes and in professional revalidation, and is judged on depth of analysis and professional judgement, not on confession.
masteryEvidence: Keeps the descriptive stage brief and anonymises people and settings in line with professional confidentiality requirements
Moves between past tense for the event, present tense for analysis and theory, and future or modal forms for the action plan
Explains why something happened by linking the experience to research, theory or professional standards, not only to personal feelings
Acknowledges own contribution and limitations in a professional, measured register
Produces an action plan with specific, achievable changes linked to the analysis
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 300-word student reflection that is two-thirds description and ends with 'I learned a lot and will do better next time'. Ask them to identify what the marker would criticise and to rewrite the ending. Check whether they spot the imbalance between description and analysis, the absence of literature, and the vague action plan, and whether their rewrite proposes a specific change linked to an identified cause.

topics.name: Case reports and care plans
topics.description: Produce the case-based genres of health education: oral and written case presentations that order patient information conventionally (presenting complaint, history, examination, investigations, assessment, plan), and care plans that link assessed needs to goals, interventions with rationales, and evaluation. These genres select and order information for clinical decision-making, use standard abbreviations cautiously and must respect confidentiality.
masteryEvidence: Presents a case in the conventional order used by the programme, selecting information relevant to the clinical problem rather than recounting everything
Writes goals that are specific, measurable and patient-centred, and links each intervention to a goal with a rationale supported by evidence
Distinguishes subjective information from objective findings, and findings from interpretation
Uses only abbreviations approved locally and expands those that could be misread
Anonymises patient details and uses respectful, person-centred language
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a disordered set of notes about a fictional patient and ask them to deliver a two-minute case presentation. Check whether they follow the expected order, foreground information relevant to the presenting problem, separate findings from interpretation, and end with an assessment and plan.

topics.name: Professional communication in health placements
topics.description: Communicate safely and appropriately with patients, families and colleagues on placement: structuring consultations, asking open and closed questions, explaining in lay terms and checking understanding, responding to emotion, seeking consent, and giving concise structured handovers or escalations to colleagues. On placement, language is part of clinical safety and is assessed against professional standards; it also involves understanding colloquial and regional ways patients describe symptoms.
masteryEvidence: Explains a procedure or condition to a lay person without unexplained jargon and checks understanding by asking the person to say it back in their own words
Uses open questions to elicit a patient's account and closed questions to clarify specific details
Acknowledges a patient's concern or emotion before giving information
Gives a concise structured handover or escalation in the format used on the placement
Recognises common colloquial descriptions of symptoms and clarifies them rather than guessing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Role-play a three-minute exchange in which the learner explains a simple procedure (for example taking a blood pressure reading) to an anxious patient who uses a colloquial expression. Check for lay terminology, an acknowledgement of the concern, a clarification question about the expression and a check of understanding that asks the patient to explain back rather than 'Do you understand?'.

topics.name: Critical appraisal and systematic review writing
topics.description: Appraise health research with a structured tool suited to the study design (for example a CASP checklist) and write up the appraisal as a reasoned judgement about validity, results and applicability. At more advanced levels, report systematic or structured reviews transparently, following reporting guidance such as PRISMA 2020 for search, selection, risk-of-bias assessment and synthesis. Appraisal assignments are common in health programmes and are marked on judgement, not on checklist completion.
masteryEvidence: Selects an appraisal tool appropriate to the study design and justifies the choice
Turns checklist answers into continuous prose that weighs strengths and weaknesses and reaches an overall judgement about trustworthiness and applicability
Uses appraisal vocabulary accurately (risk of bias, confounding, generalisability, attrition, blinding)
Calibrates claims about findings to study quality
Reports a review's search, screening and selection process transparently, including a flow diagram where expected
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract and methods summary of a small randomised trial with one clear weakness (for example high attrition without intention-to-treat analysis). Ask for a 150-word appraisal paragraph. Check whether they identify the weakness, explain its likely effect on the result, balance it against strengths and reach a calibrated conclusion about applying the findings.

topics.name: Business case analysis
topics.description: Write a business case analysis or case report: identify the central problem in an organisational case, analyse its causes with appropriate frameworks and the data in the case, generate and evaluate options against explicit criteria, and make justified, feasible recommendations for a named decision-maker. The genre is problem- and decision-oriented rather than thesis-led and is among the most common assessments in business schools.
masteryEvidence: States the central problem of the case in one or two sentences and distinguishes it from its symptoms
Uses case data and exhibits as evidence for each analytic point, with explicit interpretation
Generates at least two realistic options and evaluates each against stated criteria such as cost, feasibility, risk and fit with strategy
Makes recommendations that follow from the analysis and include implementation considerations
States assumptions where the case information is incomplete
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page mini-case and 20 minutes. Ask for a problem statement, two options and a recommendation in note form. Check whether the problem is a cause rather than a symptom, whether options are evaluated against criteria and whether the recommendation follows from the evaluation rather than from general opinion.

topics.name: Language of economic reasoning
topics.description: Control the language economists use to reason with models: stating assumptions, holding other factors constant (ceteris paribus), conditional and counterfactual predictions, comparative statics (what happens to equilibrium when one variable changes), marginal reasoning, and the distinction between positive and normative statements. It also includes describing diagrams precisely (a shift of a curve versus a movement along it) and distinguishing causal from correlational claims in empirical economics.
masteryEvidence: States the assumptions of a model before using it to predict an outcome
Uses ceteris paribus and conditional structures accurately to express what a model predicts when one variable changes
Distinguishes a shift of a curve from a movement along it in describing a diagram
Separates positive (descriptive or predictive) from normative (evaluative) statements in their own writing
Qualifies empirical claims to reflect whether the evidence is causal or correlational
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a supply-and-demand diagram in which a tax shifts the supply curve. Ask them to explain in writing what happens to price and quantity and why. Check for explicit assumptions or ceteris paribus, correct use of shift versus movement along, conditional or causal sequencing, and avoidance of normative judgement unless asked.

topics.name: Professional business genres
topics.description: Write and present the simulated professional genres business schools assess: memos, briefing notes, management reports and pitches.
